# LACE-UP: An ensemble machine-learning method for health subtype classification on multidimensional binary data

**Authors:** Rebecca Danning; Frank B. Hu; Xihong Lin

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Biostatistics, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA 02215 | bDepartment of Nutritional Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA 02215 | cDepartment of Statistics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138

## Abstract

Cluster analysis can be used on symptom and behavior data to identify groups of similar individuals who may share underlying disease etiology or health risks. However, there are few clustering methods for binary data, which are common in self-reported lifestyle and behavior symptom data, meaning many of these subtypes remain undetected. To address this methodological gap, we propose LACE-UP, an ensemble machine-learning method for subtype detection from binary data. We show in simulations that LACE-UP can recover latent subtypes under realistic data conditions better than existing methods and that it uncovers clinically significant subtypes from real self-reported health behavior data. These findings show the potential LACE-UP has for enabling etiologic discovery and improving care by refining patient diagnoses.

## Abstract

Disease and behavior subtype identification is of significant interest in biomedical research. However, in many settings, subtype discovery is limited by a lack of robust statistical clustering methods appropriate for binary data. Here, we introduce LACE-UP [latent class analysis ensembled with UMAP (uniform manifold approximation and projection) and PCA (principal components analysis)], an ensemble machine-learning method for clustering multidimensional binary data that does not require prespecifying the number of clusters and is robust to realistic data settings, such as the correlation of variables observed from the same individual and the inclusion of variables unrelated to the underlying subtype. The method ensembles latent class analysis, a model-based clustering method; principal components analysis, a spectral signal processing method; and UMAP, a cutting-edge model-free dimensionality reduction algorithm. In simulations, LACE-UP outperforms gold-standard techniques across a variety of realistic scenarios, including in the presence of correlated and extraneous data. We apply LACE-UP to dietary behavior data from the UK Biobank to demonstrate its power to uncover interpretable dietary subtypes that are associated with lipids and cardiovascular risk.

The identification of disease and behavior subtypes is a critical goal in health science research. Identifying groups of similar subjects can allow for targeted treatments, improved disease management, informed policy decisions, and discovery of heterogeneous biological mechanisms underlying the subtypes (1–4). When subjects can be classified based on the presence of a biomarker, the identification of subtypes is straightforward. However, interest often lies in classifying subjects with respect to symptoms or behavioral patterns as opposed to biology. For example, individuals can be classified by health behavior profiles, such as diet and exercise habits, to find subgroups to target for lifestyle-based interventions (5–7). Many studies have used statistical cluster analysis methods on multidimensional measurement data to uncover these subtypes (8). The choice of clustering method depends on the data type and the underlying goals of the study; statistical methods used for this purpose include Gaussian finite mixture modeling (9, 10), principal components analysis (11, 12), hierarchical cluster analysis (13), and k -means clustering (14, 15).

When observed data are binary, latent class analysis (LCA) is a popular choice for investigating subtypes (16–18). Many lifestyle variables are binary, such as physical inactivity or smoking status; identifying subtypes of individuals on the basis of these behaviors allows for the identification of individuals who are at increased risk for disease or premature mortality (19–21). Similarly, many psychiatric conditions are diagnosed based on presence versus absence of several behavioral symptoms. Identifying subtypes within these diagnoses allows for the refinement of otherwise highly heterogeneous phenotypes (1, 8, 22). In a binary data setting, LCA outperforms the two other commonly used methods, k -means clustering and hierarchical clustering (23–25). Additionally, the LCA model has an intuitive interpretation in the context of disease subtypes: it posits subpopulations (the latent classes or subtypes), each of which is internally homogeneous with respect to the observed variables (the symptoms/behaviors) (26).

However, there are several potential drawbacks to LCA. In a real data context, researchers may include observed data in analysis that are not related to an underlying subtype. As with other clustering methods, the inclusion of variables that have no relationship to class membership may obscure the true underlying cluster structure and can lead to biased estimators (27, 28). Another challenge in real data contexts is the conditional independence assumption. In its simplest form, LCA also assumes that responses are independent conditional on class membership such that conditioning on the latent class, observations are homogeneous in subpopulations and any correlation structure among the variables is removed (26). However, in the context of real symptom or behavior data, observations may be heterogeneous in subpopulations, and there may be individual-level factors outside of class membership that influence whether or not a variable is observed, such as a subjective reporting threshold or barriers to accessing care. Methods extending LCA to allow for a relaxation of the conditional independence assumption generally rely on modeling the dependence directly (29–31), which presents challenges for estimation (32), and standard software implementations have not yet incorporated these extensions (33–35).

Potentially the most significant challenge to LCA, along with other methods such as k -means clustering and hierarchical clustering, is that its results are sensitive to the number of classes/clusters selected by the researcher (“class enumeration”). While standard statistical software packages for running LCA provide fit statistics for each model (33), there is often disagreement among the various goodness-of-fit statistics (36), and the goodness-of-fit statistics are usually biased toward models with more classes and diminished interpretability (37). Additionally, the assumptions underlying the goodness-of-fit statistics may be invalidated by sparsely distributed contingency tables, such as when there are only a few occurrences of particular response patterns (38). Choosing an incorrect value for the number of classes can yield misleading results that may have little relationship to the truth (39).

In this paper, we introduce LACE-UP [latent class analysis ensembled with UMAP (uniform manifold approximation and projection) and PCA], an ensemble method for detecting subtypes from binary data that overcomes the deficiencies of LCA and makes use of recent advances in high-dimensional clustering methodology. Unlike traditional implementations of LCA and other clustering methods such as k -means clustering and hierarchical clustering, LACE-UP does not require the researcher to choose the number of clusters ahead of time (“ k -agnostic”). Instead, the method takes advantage of the variance-reducing properties of ensemble learning (40) and utilizes multiple LCA models, extracting and concatenating the principal components of each model’s full posterior probability matrix. This projects the binary data onto the continuous joint latent space comprising the combined insights from each constituent model. The data can then be reduced into low-dimensional space with uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (41), an advanced nonparametric, nonlinear machine-learning algorithm for dimensionality reduction that likewise does not require selecting the number of clusters in advance. UMAP has gained traction for its success in a variety of applied settings, as well as its improved performance over t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) for clustering purposes (42, 43). However, as we will demonstrate, UMAP applied directly to binary data is less robust to noise than methods grounded in statistical models.

LACE-UP is a robust method for clustering binary data that incorporates the intuitive model-based insights of LCA while avoiding the pitfalls inherent in prespecifying the number of clusters. Rather than selecting an optimal number of classes, LACE-UP combines the insights from multiple models, yielding a k -agnostic ensemble result that outperforms any single underlying LCA model under realistic data-generating scenarios (SI Appendix, Fig. S4). We present simulations that show LACE-UP outperforms the existing techniques in the presence of extraneous variables and local dependence, both of which are expected in real-world health data settings. We also demonstrate the practical utility of LACE-UP on the UK Biobank dietary questionnaire data, where the algorithm yields interpretable dietary clusters. We show significant associations of the estimated dietary subtypes with blood lipid levels and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

## Results

### Overview of LACE-UP.

LACE-UP is a machine-learning method that ensembles multiple LCA models using spectral and nonlinear dimensionality reduction algorithms. Rather than requiring the investigator to choose a hypothesized number of latent classes, LACE-UP allows the researcher to incorporate insights from a variety of candidate models in a manner that avoids the bias associated with misspecifying the number of classes. As shown in Fig. 1, LACE-UP first runs LCA on the input data with a range of values of the number of classes k . The output of each of these models is an n × k posterior probability matrix, where each row contains the posterior probability of an individual belonging to each of the k classes. As such, the posterior probability matrix can be thought of as the embedding of the individuals in k -dimensional latent space. The goal is to find clusters of individuals across the joint latent space combining the insights from each of the candidate models.

*Fig. 1.: Framework of LACE-UP. The input data are observations of p binary variables from n individuals. First, we run k -class LCA for each of the candidate values of k ; in this example, the candidate values of k are k = { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } . Each LCA model yields a n × k posterior probability matrix containing each individual’s posterior probability of belonging to each of the k classes. Second, we calculate the principal components of each of the posterior probability matrices. Third, these principal component matrices are concatenated, yielding the joint principal component matrix PC. We then run UMAP on PC to obtain a two-dimensional embedding of the joint model summary space and automate cluster extraction with dbscan .*

To do this, we first calculate the principal components of the posterior probability matrices for the purpose of signal amplification and noise reduction. An underspecified model may comprise an agglomeration of the true clusters and therefore contain signal; likewise, an overspecified model may contain both signal and noise if, for example, true clusters are falsely partitioned. As UMAP is based on a nearest-neighbor graph, the idea is that the principal components representing signal are reinforced in the calculations of nearest neighbors and the noisy principal components are averaged out. Concatenating the principal components of the posterior probability matrices for input into UMAP leads to the amplification of signal contained in the posterior probability matrices, allowing for clusters to be found within the joint latent space. The sensitivity analyses with respect to the largest number of classes being considered K ∗ shown in SI Appendix, Fig. S1A show that performance improves as K ∗ increases, supporting the proposition that the true signal is amplified and the noise diminished through this procedure. However, the incremental benefit decreases as K ∗ increases, and as shown in SI Appendix, Fig. S1B, there is a penalty in terms of computational time for increasing K ∗ , so the choice of K ∗ must be balanced against computational limitations. We provide further details about LACE-UP and its component parts in Materials and Methods.

### Simulation Setup.

We evaluate the performance of LACE-UP under six simulation settings. For each simulation, we postulate four underlying subtypes, which in this case we will think of as diseases giving rise to symptoms. We simulate 1,000 subjects from each of the four subtypes for a total of 4,000 patients. For each subject, we observe data on the presence or absence of each of twelve binary symptoms. There are 2 × 3 simulation settings:

#### Conditional independence vs. local dependence.

In the conditional independence setting, responses are generated based solely on subtype membership, meaning the latent class model is correctly specified. However, since this model is unrealistic for real data, we also simulate data in a local dependence setting where responses are correlated within individuals conditional on subtype memberships. To do this, we move to a data-generating model inspired by the liability threshold model (44). We also take into account that different individuals have different thresholds for reporting symptoms. For example, for symptoms, this can be due to differing perceptions of severity, such as pain tolerances, access to care, trust in the health system, or other reasons. We establish a threshold value for each subject and thus only observe dichotomized versions of the true underlying severity data. This means that conditional on subtype membership, responses within an individual are correlated due to the individual’s unique reporting threshold, i.e., for subject i , different severity scores s ip share the same threshold u i , which can be viewed as an individual-specific random threshold.

#### All relevant symptoms vs. 1/3 nuisance symptoms vs. 1/2 nuisance symptoms.

In the setting where all symptoms are relevant, we simulate data such that all symptoms are generated from a probability distribution related to disease subtype. Realistically, however, there may be cases in which extraneous data unrelated to the underlying subtype is analyzed. To evaluate the robustness of the methods to variables unrelated to the underlying subtype, we allow one-third and one-half of the symptoms to be “nuisance variables,” or symptoms for which the probability distribution is unrelated to the underlying subtype.

We compare LACE-UP to 4-class LCA (the oracle method when the model is correctly specified), k -means clustering with k = 4 , hierarchical clustering with k = 4 , UMAP with the Hamming distance (appropriate for binary data), and t-SNE. In all of these simulations, we evaluate each method’s performance via normalized mutual information. Normalized mutual information is a measure from 0 to 1 that computes how accurately the derived cluster labels recover the true underlying subtype. The mathematical details of the simulations can be found in Materials and Methods.

### Simulation Results.

The main simulation results are shown in Fig. 2. When conditional independence holds, the oracle LCA method consistently performs best, even in the presence of nuisance variables, followed by LACE-UP and k -means clustering. The performance of hierarchical clustering diminishes severely with the introduction of nuisance symptoms and is consistently the worst of the three oracle methods. UMAP and t-SNE perform fairly consistently across the conditional independence settings, although t-SNE is more sensitive to the introduction of nuisance symptoms. Both methods are outperformed by oracle LCA, LACE-UP, and oracle k-means in all conditional independence settings. When LCA is no longer correctly specified due to local dependence, but all included input variables are relevant to the underlying subtypes, the results are similar to the conditional independence setting with no nuisance symptoms. The results for the most realistic simulations, those with both local dependence and nuisance input variables, are found in the bottom center and bottom right sections of Fig. 2. Under the local dependence setting, LACE-UP is the only method that is robust to the introduction of nuisance symptoms, and clearly outperforms all other methods.

The simulations in the top row maintain the LCA assumption of conditional independence, and the simulations in the bottom row incorporate correlation of observed variables within individuals. As shown in SI Appendix, Fig. S4, which compares LACE-UP to misspecified LCA models, in this case overspecifying the number of latent classes yields improved performance compared to the 4-class model, but LACE-UP outperforms even the overspecified latent class models. When conditional independence is violated, k -means clustering performs similarly to vanilla LCA. The performance of hierarchical clustering remains poor compared to other methods. The two methods that are not affected by the introduction of nuisance symptoms in the presence of local dependence are LACE-UP and t-SNE, although the performance of t-SNE is consistently much worse than LACE-UP.

Finally, it is important to note that LCA, k -means clustering, and hierarchical clustering are all oracle methods, meaning they are run assuming one knows the true number of clusters, which would not occur in real data analysis. LACE-UP is the most robust and powerful method for recovering the latent subtype structure in the presence of local dependence and nuisance variables, both of which are highly realistic in real data settings, and does not require oracle knowledge of the number of subtypes.

#### Expanded simulations.

To explore further how the performance of LACE-UP changes based on other parameters, such as the total number of symptoms and class membership imbalance, we conducted additional simulations within the setting of local dependence and 1/2 nuisance symptoms. The results of these simulations are shown in Fig. 3. In each simulation setting, the default settings are as in the main simulations: k = 4 clusters, 12 symptoms, equal distribution of individuals between the classes, and an underlying B e t a ( 8 , 3 ) distribution for the high-probability symptoms. In Fig. 3A, we increase the number of total symptoms (only half of which are relevant to the underlying classes), and we see that the performance of all methods increases. Notably, once there are a total of 24 symptoms, UMAP starts to outperform LACE-UP; however, LACE-UP outperforms all other methods across all numbers of symptoms.

### Dietary Patterns in the UK Biobank.

Dietary pattern analysis has emerged as a valuable tool in nutritional epidemiology. Rather than examining the effects of single nutrients or food groups on health outcomes, dietary pattern analysis instead examines the relationships between patterns of eating behavior and disease outcomes, which in turn leads to intuitive and actionable guidelines for public health (45). We examine the ability of LACE-UP to detect clinically relevant dietary patterns using dietary intake data from the UK Biobank for 170,966 unrelated British White individuals who have not changed their diet in the past five years using fifteen categories of food, dichotomized by whether an individual reports that food group to be part of their regular diet (the full list of food categories and details on the dichotomization can be found in SI Appendix).

The clustering results from LACE-UP are shown in Fig. 4. Fig. 4A shows the lower-dimensional embedding and cluster assignment resulting from LACE-UP, and Fig. 4B shows the prevalence of each food category for each cluster. Looking across the rows of Fig. 4B, one can see that the clusters are primarily delineated by the meat and fish variables, whereas other variables are more consistent across clusters. This is analogous to the “nuisance variables” scenarios in the simulations, where an advantage of LACE-UP is its ability to downweight potentially unimportant input variables. Cluster 1 ( n = 161 , 661 ) is an omnivorous cluster with no strong restrictions on any category. This cluster is the largest in terms of both membership and size in the lower-dimensional embedding. Cluster 2 ( n = 3 , 540 ) is a vegetarian cluster, with almost no meat and low fish consumption. Cluster 3 ( n = 5 , 765 ) comprises primarily pescatarians, as well as some individuals who consume poultry, but almost no individuals who consume other meat types.

For comparison, we can examine the performance of standard LCA and UMAP on the data. The fit statistics associated with LCA models for k ∈ { 2 , . . . , 12 } are shown in SI Appendix, Fig. S5A. All fit statistics decrease as k increases. The AIC , BIC , and Gsq (deviance) fit statistics seem to suggest any of k = 5 , k = 7 , or k = 9 , and the chi-square goodness of fit suggests any of k = 3 , k = 5 , or k = 8 . Thus, the fit indices alone cannot fully guide model selection. To examine the interpretability of each of these models, we can look at the dietary profiles of the clusters from the models, as shown in SI Appendix, Fig. S5B. For k = 3 , Cluster 1 appears to be a low-meat cluster, and then Cluster 2 seems to have lower consumption probabilities compared to Cluster 3 on all food groups with the exception of processed meat. For k = 5 , Cluster 1 is again a low-meat cluster, and cluster 2 seems to be a fish + poultry cluster. The differentiation among clusters 3, 4, and 5 is less immediately apparent but shows the greatest differences in fish, lamb, and dried fruit. For k ≥ 7 , the clusters become increasingly difficult to interpret; notably, none of the models yield patterns as easily interpretable as those from LACE-UP. The clustering results for UMAP are shown in SI Appendix, Fig. S6. In this instance, UMAP fails to find cluster structure in the data; this may be a reflection of the diminished performance of UMAP in settings with local dependence and nuisance variables, as shown in Fig. 2.

To examine the clinical relevance of the derived diet subtypes, we ran logistic regression models of incident diseases [stroke, myocardial infarction (MI), hypertension (HBP)] and linear regression of statin-adjusted lipid measures on the estimated dietary subtypes, as shown in Fig. 4C. All models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, low vs. moderate/high physical activity, ever vs. never smoking, and socioeconomic status via the Townsend deprivation index. When examining the dietary cluster effect sizes on the lipid profiles, two notable patterns emerge. First, with statistically significant differences, the vegetarian cluster is associated with the lowest values of LDL cholesterol and total cholesterol, with the pescatarian cluster also lower than the omnivorous cluster, although not as low as the vegetarian cluster. Second, the pescatarian cluster has generally equivalent levels of HDL cholesterol as the omnivorous cluster, whereas the vegetarian cluster has lower levels of HDL, which is in line with existing research (46). Lower HDL levels are associated with higher carbohydrate intake (47), and vegetarians tend to consume more carbohydrates than those who follow omnivorous or pescatarian diets (48).

Logistic regressions of stroke ( n cases = 3 , 980 , n controls = 166 , 982 ), myocardial infarction ( n cases = 4 , 657 , n controls = 166 , 305 ), and hypertension ( n cases = 36 , 559 , n controls = 134 , 403 ) show the significant effects of dietary patterns on these disease risks. The vegetarian and pescatarian clusters show a decreased risk of incident stroke, which aligns with evidence showing red meat consumption is associated with an increased risk of stroke (49, 50). Both clusters also show a lower risk of incident myocardial infarction, although the association with the vegetarian cluster is not statistically significant. These results are consistent with the literature: a diet lower in saturated fat and higher in n − 3 polyunsaturated fat, as is a pescatarian diet compared to an omnivorous diet with red meat, is associated with significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease and thus myocardial infarction (51). Likewise, diets that restrict the consumption of animal products are associated with lower cardiovascular disease risk (52), whereas diets containing higher amounts of red and processed meat are associated with higher risk of cardiovascular disease and thus myocardial infarction (50, 53, 54). Finally, the statistically significant lower risk of incident hypertension is in line with research showing associations between vegetarian diets and lower blood pressure (46), as well as a positive association between red meat intake and hypertension (55).

The intuitive results of the LACE-UP clusters on the UK Biobank dietary application data, as well as the clusters’ associations with lipid levels and incident outcomes that reflect known phenomena in nutritional epidemiology, demonstrate that LACE-UP is able to derive clusters from binary data with both statistically and clinically significant associations to several common diseases.

## Discussion

In this paper, we introduced LACE-UP, an ensemble machine-learning method for detecting subtypes within patterns of binary symptom and behavior data. LACE-UP is k -agnostic, meaning it does not require the researcher to select the number of clusters, and is more robust to realistic binary measurement settings than existing methods, as demonstrated in our simulations and analysis of the UK Biobank data. Specifically, we showed through simulations that LACE-UP improves upon existing clustering methods in the presence of three common challenges: the erroneous inclusion of variables that are not related to the underlying subtypes, correlation of responses within each individual conditional on subtypes, and sensitivity to the choice of the number of subtypes. When applied to the UK Biobank dietary questionnaire data, LACE-UP yields diet clusters that are both easy to interpret and associated with several cardiovascular disease-related outcomes.

The ability to detect latent subtypes from binary symptom and behavioral data holds promise for disease discovery in several ways. Refining phenotypes through the detection of subtypes can yield interpretable results that help guide further study of behavioral and disease subtypes. Phenotypic refinement can also enable improved discovery of the biological mechanisms underlying each subtype. Further, refining individual classification can lead to the development of targeted treatments and interventions, improved patient guidance, and enhanced disease prevention.

One limitation of LACE-UP is its lack of framework for statistical inference due to its usage of UMAP. Since UMAP is model-free, it is unclear how to assess the variance of the clusterings or how to create CI from its output. This is in contrast to model-based dimensionality reduction methods such as principal components analysis, which can yield CI through asymptotic estimates of the variance (56). The development of paradigms for inference on the output of methods like UMAP is a valuable avenue for future research.

While many behaviors and symptoms are best described by binary variables, it is possible that researchers may be interested in incorporating other data types as well, such as continuous data representing symptom and behavior frequency. It is of future interest to extend LACE-UP to allow for such data; the current software implementation is restricted to polytomous data (33). One such possible avenue for this is to view the LCA step within the general framework of representation learning and substitute it with a mixture method approach (57). Another potential extension is to incorporate a LCA method that allows for covariates (31); this method could be especially valuable if, for example, symptom reporting threshold were related to some measured variable.

As discussed previously, an important step in any cluster analysis is interpreting the resulting clusters. The clusters resulting from the UK Biobank dietary behavior data were easy to interpret because they cohere with our existing knowledge of dietary patterns. However, not every clustering output may be so simple to interpret, either because the patterns are unexpected or because the underlying symptoms or behaviors are not well understood. Coherent descriptions of each cluster are invaluable for any translational applications of clustering algorithms, since they allow researchers to incorporate additional contextual information post hoc. Future methodology development focused on summarizing and semantically labeling the output of clustering algorithms would be a significant asset in health research.

## Materials and Methods

### LACE-UP.

#### Step 1: LCA.

Let the input data be n × p binary data representing n individuals and p binary measurements. The first step of LACE-UP is to perform LCA for a range of the number of classes k . Specifically, for k ∈ { 2 , . . . , K ∗ } , where K ∗ is the largest number of classes under consideration, perform LCA with k classes [implemented via poLCA (33) in R]. LCA is a latent variable model that makes the assumption that conditional on class membership, measurements are independently distributed and follow a Bernoulli distribution indexed by the latent class (58). The output of a latent class model with n individuals, k classes, and p measurements is a set of conditional probabilities π qj for q = 1 , . . . , p and j = 1 , . . . , k and latent class probabilities η 1 , . . . , η k . These conditional probabilities and latent class probabilities can be used to calculate an n × k posterior probability matrix ζ ^ k . Each row contains the estimated posterior probabilities of the individual belonging to each of the k classes.

For k -class LCA, let Y i 1 , . . . , Y ip be a vector of p observed binary variables for subject i and let C i ∈ { 1 , 2 , . . . , k } be the latent class to which individual i belongs: C i ∼ M u l t i n o m i a l ( { 1 , . . . , k } , { η 1 , . . . , η k } ) ,

where η k is the probability that a randomly selected individual from the population belongs to latent class k . The assumed distribution is Y iq ∣ C i = k ∼ B e r n o u l l i ( π qk ) and the observed variables Y 1 , . . . , Y p are conditionally independent given C : π qk = P ( Y iq = 1 ∣ C i = k ) .

The joint distribution of the data is P ( Y i 1 = y i 1 , . . . , Y ip = y ip ) = ∑ j = 1 k P ( Y i 1 = y i 1 , . . . , Y ip = y ip ∣ C i = j ) P ( C i = j ) = ∑ j = 1 k η j ∏ q = 1 p π qj y iq ( 1 − π qj ) 1 − y iq .

Each conditional item probability π qj and class probability η j for j ∈ { 1 , . . . , k } is estimated using the EM algorithm.

Once the conditional item and class probabilities have been estimated, the posterior probability of an individual with observed variables y i = ( y i 1 , . . . , y ip ) belonging to latent class j ∈ { 1 , . . . , k } is 12 p t P ( C i = j ∣ Y i = y i ) = P ( C i = j , Y i = y i ) P ( Y i = y i ) = P ( Y i = y i ∣ C i = j ) P ( C i = j ) ∑ j = 1 k P ( Y i = y i ∣ C i = j ) P ( C i = j ) = ∏ q = 1 p π qj y iq ( 1 − π qj ) 1 − y iq · η k ∑ j = 1 k ∏ q = 1 p π qj y iq ( 1 − π qj ) 1 − y iq · η j .

Denote ζ ij = P ( C i = j ∣ Y i = y i ) . Let ζ ^ ij be the estimated posterior probability of individual i belonging to latent class j . Define ζ ^ ik = ( ζ ^ i 1 , ⋯ , ζ ^ ik ) T , and let ζ ^ k be a n × k matrix that contains all of the estimated posterior class membership probabilities of the n subjects obtained from fitting a latent class model with k classes for k = 2 , ⋯ , K ∗ .

#### Step 2: Principal components analysis.

As the goal of LACE-UP is to consider multiple latent class models simultaneously, the next step is to combine the ζ ^ k matrices. A straightforward concatenation of these matrices is suboptimal given that, particularly in the case of overspecified models, many of the classes may be spurious (this is less of a concern in the underspecified case where classes may be agglomerations of the true classes and therefore contain signal). However, an overspecified model may also contain signal, for example if true classes are split into false subclasses. We can utilize principal component analysis to extract the main axes of variation from the posterior probability matrices in the hope that noisy axes average out in the subsequent UMAP nearest neighbor graph stage. Thus, for each k , we calculate the principal components of the n × k matrix ζ ^ k . Denote these PCs by W k . Collect all of these PCs from k = 2 , ⋯ , K ∗ and denote them by P C = ( W 2 , W 3 , ⋯ , W K ∗ ) .

#### Step 3: UMAP.

The third step of LACE-UP is to apply UMAP to P C to reduce its dimensionality for clustering. UMAP is a topological machine-learning method for dimensionality reduction (41). There are two main steps to UMAP: first, UMAP creates a high-dimensional fuzzy topological representation of the data via a nearest-neighbors graph, then finds its best low-dimensional representation (59).

#### Constructing a fuzzy topological representation.

A critical hyperparameter in UMAP is the number of nearest neighbors z . The first step in UMAP is to create a z -nearest neighbors graph where every point has an edge of weight 1 to its nearest neighbor, then a diminishing weight to its next nearest z − 1 neighbors.

For a data point x i , let x i 1 , . . . , x i z be its z nearest neighbors according to a distance metric. Let ρ i be the distance between x i and its nearest neighbor. Define a normalization factor σ i such that ∑ j = 1 z exp − max ( 0 , d i s t ( x i , x i j ) − ρ i ) σ i = log 2 ( z ) .

Define a weighted directed multigraph G ¯ = ( V , E , w ) , where V is the set of data points x i , E is the set of edges between each x i and its z nearest neighbors, and w is the edge weight function w ( x i , x i j ) = exp − max ( 0 , d i s t ( x i , x i j ) − ρ i ) σ i .

Each point has its own weighting function based on how close its nearest neighbors are, and so there are two edges between points s and t : an edge from s to t with weight w ( s , t ) and an edge from t to s with weight w ( t , s ) . The algorithm converts the weighted directed multigraph G ¯ to a weighted undirected graph G by combining the weights. Let w G ¯ ( s , t ) = a and w G ¯ ( t , s ) = b , then w G ( s , t ) = w G ( s , t ) = a + b − a · b . Thinking of edge weights as probabilities, this is the probability that at least one of the two edges exists.

This process can be thought of in topological terms as constructing an open cover (union of sets that cover the entire space) from 0-simplices (nodes) and 1-simplices (edges). The Nerve Theorem guarantees that a nearest-neighbor graph constructed as above is a “good enough” open cover representation of the underlying manifold or structure. However, the Nerve Theorem requires the points to be uniformly distributed on the underlying manifold, which typically is not the case with real data. This is the rationale behind each data point having its own distance metric; we can impose the uniform distribution of the data by defining the unique distance metrics relative to each point such that every point is equally distant to its z th nearest neighbor. Additionally, defining the nearest neighbors graph with respect to relative distance as opposed to absolute distance helps UMAP avoid the curse of dimensionality and makes it more robust to higher-dimensional data (59).

#### Finding the closest low-dimensional representation.

Once the topological representation from step 1 has been created, the next step is to project that representation onto the desired low-dimensional space. The algorithm does this by examining all possible low-dimensional graphs that consist of the same set of nodes as the high-dimensional graph, then examining which low-dimensional graph is most similar in terms of cross-entropy.

Let V be the set of nodes or data points in the high-dimensional G from step 1, let E G be the set of edges of G , and for e ∈ E G , define q G ( e ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] as the weight of the edge in G . Next, let E ∗ be the set of all possible edges between points in V (for a total of | V | 2 edges). Let G be the set of all lower-dimensional (usually two-dimensional) graphs with the same set of nodes as G . Define q g ( e ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] to be the weight associated with e ∈ E ∗ for graph g ∈ G .

For each potential lower-dimensional graph g ∈ G , compare graph g with G via cross entropy: H ( G , g ) = ∑ e ∈ E ∗ q G ( e ) log q G ( e ) q g ( e ) + ( 1 − q G ( e ) ) log 1 − q G ( e ) 1 − q g ( e ) .

The best lower-dimensional embedding is the g ∈ G that minimizes H ( G , g ) . Thus, the output of applying UMAP to the 2 ( K ∗ − 1 ) -dimensional matrix P C yields its best two-dimensional representation, which can then be used for clustering, either manually or with an algorithm such as dbscan (60).

### Mathematical Details of the Simulation Settings.

In the conditional independence setting with no nuisance symptoms, for each of p ∈ { 1 , . . . , 12 } binary symptom variables s ip , its value for individual i with subtype d is drawn from s ip ∼ B e r n o u l l i ( π p ( d ) ) with π p ( d ) ∈ { 0.9 , 0.1 } . In other words, the probability of an individual having the p th symptom is fully specified by the underlying subtype d : P ( s ip = 1 ) = π p ( d ) . Let π ( d ) = ( π 1 ( d ) , . . . , π 12 ( d ) ) ∈ { 0.1 , 0.9 } 12 represent the 12-tuple of probabilities for class d . For each of the 1,000 simulations, we draw the π ( d ) s without replacement from { 0.1 , 0.9 } 12 such that no two subtypes have the same distribution of probabilities. Likewise, in the case that all π p ( d ) s are equal for some p , we randomly select one d to change such that all of the symptom probabilities vary across subtypes.

In the conditional independence setting when 1/3 of variables are nuisance, for p ∈ { 1 , . . . , 8 } we have s ip ∼ B e r n o u l l i ( π p ( d ) ) as before. However, for p ∈ { 9 , . . . , 12 } , we set s ip ∼ B e r n o u l l i ( 0.5 ) , so the likelihood of an individual having these nuisance variables is no longer related to the underlying subtype. In this case, we draw the π ( d ) s without replacement from { 0.1 , 0.9 } 9 , randomly modifying as before to ensure all symptom probabilities vary across subtypes, and then append (0.5,0.5,0.5) to each 9-tuple. When 1/2 of variables are nuisance, the same procedure applies, except with six randomly selected probabilities and six probabilities set at 0.5.

In the local dependence settings, for individual i with subtype d , we draw a continuous underlying severity value in [0,1] for binary symptom variable p from s ip ∗ ∼ B e t a ( α p ( d ) , β p ( d ) ) with ( α p ( d ) , β p ( d ) ) ∈ { ( 8 , 3 ) , ( 3 , 8 ) } . We follow the same procedure as in the conditional independence setting to ensure that symptom profiles are unique and each nonnuisance symptom varies across the subtypes. The underlying liability distribution for binary symptom variable p is fully specified by the individual’s underlying subtype d . For each of the 1,000 simulations, for each combination of d and p , ( α p ( d ) , β p ( d ) ) is randomly chosen from { ( 8 , 3 ) , ( 3 , 8 ) } . The threshold value is drawn from u i ∼ U n i f o r m [ 0.3 , 0.7 ] and we observe s ip = I ( s ip ∗ ≥ u i ) . The probability of an individual having symptom p is specified by both the underlying subtype d and the individual’s threshold: for individual i of subtype d and reporting threshold u i , the probability of observing variable p is P ( s ip = 1 ) = ∫ u i 1 Γ ( α p ( d ) + β p ( d ) ) Γ ( α p ( d ) ) Γ ( β p ( d ) ) s α p ( d ) − 1 ( 1 − s ) β p ( d ) − 1 d s .

In practice, this means that the probability ranges from 0.617 to 0.998 in the case of an underlying B e t a ( 8 , 3 ) distribution and 0.002 to 0.383 in the case of an underlying B e t a ( 3 , 8 ) distribution, depending on the individual’s threshold. The nuisance variables are drawn from a liability distribution of B e t a ( 10 , 10 ) unrelated to the underlying subtype.

For all simulations, there is no preset pattern as to which of the nonnuisance symptoms are high probability and which are low probability; each are selected randomly. As such, simulations have a random level of “difficulty” in how distinct the symptom profiles for each class are.

### Simulation Hyperparameters.

For all analyses, LCA was performed using the poLCA (33) package in R and UMAP was performed using the umap (61) package in R, which is a wrapper for the original umap (62) package in Python.

For 4-class LCA, we assign class membership based on the modal posterior probability class, as is standard. For the ensemble method, we set K ∗ = 20 . While the default distance metric used for constructing the nearest neighbor graph is Euclidean distance, we use Manhattan distance, which is shown to perform better in higher dimensions (63). Prior to running UMAP on the joint principal components matrix, we remove duplicate rows; a more detailed justification of this step is found in SI Appendix, Fig. S3. The duplicate individuals are assigned to the same cluster as that of their remaining representative. For UMAP, we use the Hamming distance metric, which is intended for binary data and defines the distance between two binary vectors as the number of times they differ element-wise. For binary data, the Hamming distance metric is equivalent to the Manhattan distance metric used in the ensemble method; see Supporting Information for further exploration of UMAP methods.

There are two hyperparameters involved in the UMAP and dbscan that we standardized for all simulations. For all UMAP implementations, the n _ n e i g h b o r s parameter is set to 0.1 × n rows , where n rows is the number of rows in the input dataset. The n _ n e i g h b o r s parameter establishes the number of nearest neighbors UMAP uses to create the high-dimensional nearest neighbors graph (41). Broadly speaking, the n _ n e i g h b o r s parameter is a trade-off between exploring more of the underlying manifold and runtime. Preliminary simulations showed that for varying values of n _ n e i g h b o r s = θ × n rows , θ = 0.1 was the lowest value that achieved the maximal accuracy. Additionally, preliminary simulations showed that extracting clusters with dbscan (60) using e p s = 1 provided consistent results. The eps parameter represents how close two points need to be in the lower-dimensional UMAP representation in order to be considered neighbors; this can be specified more carefully in an application setting.

### Normalized Mutual Information.

To measure the performance of each method for a given simulation, we calculate the normalized mutual information of the true underlying subtypes and the derived cluster labels. Given a vector of true subtypes D and a vector of derived cluster labels C , the normalized mutual information is (64): N M I ( D , C ) = 2 × I ( D , C ) H ( D ) + H ( C ) .

The mutual information I is a symmetric measure indicating how much is known about D given C , or vice versa. Let d be the number of true underlying subtypes and c be the number of derived clusters. Let n be the total number of individuals, n k d be the number of individuals with subtype k , let n j c be the number of individuals in cluster j and let n kj dc be the number of individuals with subtype k in cluster j . I ( D , C ) = ∑ k = 1 d ∑ j = 1 c n kj dc n log n kj dc n n k d n · n j c n = ∑ k = 1 d ∑ j = 1 c n kj dc n log n kj dc · n n k d · n j c .

The entropy H is a measure of the amount of uncertainty in the variable (65): H ( D ) = − ∑ k = 1 d n k d n log n k d n H ( C ) = − ∑ j = 1 c n j c n log n j c n .

It can be shown that I ( D , C ) ≤ m i n { H ( D ) , H ( C ) } (66); as such, 0 ≤ N M I ( D , C ) ≤ 1 .

In this simulation, NMI is calculated using the implementation in the package igraph (67). Let N be a confusion matrix where N kj is the number of individuals with subtype k assigned to cluster j . N M I ( N ) = − 2 ∑ k = 1 d ∑ j = 1 c N kj log N ij N N k · N · j ∑ k = 1 d N i · log N k · N + ∑ j = 1 c N · j log N · j N .

In the above equation, N is the number of individuals, N k · is the sum of row k , N · j is the sum of column j , d is the number of underlying diseases, and c is the number of clusters found by the algorithm (68).

### Data Analysis in the UK Biobank.

For our analysis, we restricted the UK Biobank study population to individuals of British White ancestry who answered “no” to the question “Have you made any major changes to your diet in the last 5 y?” and who had not withdrawn consent for analysis. We further removed instances of related individuals from the data, leaving a total of 170,966 individuals. Pedigrees of related individuals were found using the algorithm described in the PC-AiR paper (69), and one individual was randomly selected from each pedigree, yielding a set of independent subjects each with less than fourth-degree relatedness. The questionnaire data come from the Diet questionnaire (Category ID 100052). The selected survey items and their dichotomization criteria are provided in Supporting Information. Due to the size of the dataset, we set K ∗ = 12 . As in the simulations, we set the proportion for the nearest neighbors parameter at 0.1 and we set the eps parameter for dbscan to be 1.

Polygenic scores (PGSs) for body mass index (BMI) may guide early prevention and targeted treatment of obesity. Using genetic data from up to 5.1 million people (4.6% African ancestry, 14.4% American ancestry, 8.4% East Asian ancestry, 71.1% European ancestry and 1.5% South Asian ancestry) from the GIANT consortium and 23andMe, Inc., we developed ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry PGSs. The multi-ancestry score explained 17.6% of BMI variation among UK Biobank participants of European ancestry. For other populations, this ranged from 16% in East Asian-Americans to 2.2% in rural Ugandans. In the ALSPAC study, children with higher PGSs showed accelerated BMI gain from age 2.5 years to adolescence, with earlier adiposity rebound. Adding the PGS to predictors available at birth nearly doubled explained variance for BMI from age 5 onward (for example, from 11% to 21% at age 8). Up to age 5, adding the PGS to early-life BMI improved prediction of BMI at age 18 (for example, from 22% to 35% at age 5). Higher PGSs were associated with greater adult weight gain. In intensive lifestyle intervention trials, individuals with higher PGSs lost modestly more weight in the first year (0.55 kg per s.d.) but were more likely to regain it. Overall, these data show that PGSs have the potential to improve obesity prediction, particularly when implemented early in life.

Obesity is a major public health concern that causes or exacerbates many chronic diseases and leads to reduced life expectancy1–3. By 2035, more than half of the global population is projected to be living with overweight or obesity4. Although intensive lifestyle interventions (ILIs), bariatric surgery and weight loss medications are effective treatment options5,6, they are not without risk and likely to remain inaccessible to most people. Thus, preventing obesity remains paramount. In contrast to many other chronic conditions, obesity often manifests itself during childhood and tends to persist into adulthood7–9. Therefore, predictors available in early life, such as genetic variants, which are fixed at conception, could be of particular value. In recent years, PGSs that capture an individual’s inherited polygenic susceptibility to a trait or disease have shown great promise in enhancing disease

risk prediction and population screening10,11. However, it remains unclear how, when and under what circumstances PGSs for obesity might demonstrate utility for risk prediction. The widely used PGS for obesity by Khera et al.12, based on a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of BMI in over 339,000 people of predominantly European ancestry, explains approximately 8.5% of the variation in BMI in adults. However, as a PGS based on one ancestry population may have weak transferability to other ancestry populations13,14, there is a growing recognition that PGSs that represent a broad range of populations are needed to ensure quality healthcare for all15. Results Selecting the best-performing PGS To develop a PGS for BMI, we used GWAS meta-analysis summary statistics for BMI from over 200 studies from the GIANT consortium and 23andMe (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2), excluding eight studies used for tuning parameters and for testing performance (Methods). Predicting prevalent obesity in adulthood Having tuned parameters in a subset of the UKBB, we took PGSLC forward to independent validation populations, estimating the prediction accuracy for BMI and obesity in 482,135 participants from the UKBB, the Million Veteran Program (MVP)19,20, the BioMe Biobank21 and the Uganda General Population Cohort (GPC-UGR)22. Individuals were grouped by population group (AMR 22,612, AFR 29,454, EAS 1,617, EUR 423,420, SAS 1,164 and non-Hispanic Asian (AS) 4,201) (MVP-specific population label) (Methods and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). The prevalence of obesity varied substantially across populations and cohorts, with those having obesity class I or higher (that is, BMI ≥ 30 kg m−2 in AFR, AMR and EUR populations and BMI ≥ 27.5 kg m−2 for Asian-like ancestry populations23) ranging from 4.3% for the GPC-UGR to more than 45% for all ancestry subgroups in the MVP

and mean BMI ranging from 22.2 kg m−2 to 30.6 kg m2 (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 4). The performance of the PGSLC was highest in individuals of European-like ancestry from the UKBB, with an explained variance of 17.6%. A pronounced lower performance was seen for populations with greater proportions of African-like ancestry, with the explained variance being 6.3% and 5.1% in African American populations (from BioMe and MVP, respectively) and 2.2% in the GPC-UGR population from rural southwestern Uganda (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 7). Overall, we observed a median explained variance of 10.3% across our testing populations. Compared to the previously reported PGS by Khera et al. (PGSKhera)12, which was based on a smaller BMI GWAS of up to 339,224 individuals of primarily European ancestry24, we observed a 1.9–2.6-fold increase in explained variance for BMI (Fig. 2b). Childhood and adolescence We investigated whether PGSLC has predictive value at an early age within the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), a geographically homogeneous prospective birth cohort from the southwest of England with follow-up until early adulthood (Methods and Supplementary Table 3)27–29. Repeated cross-sectional associations with BMI showed small effects for PGSLC soon after birth with much stronger effects emerging in early childhood, from 0.12 s.d. per s.d. of PGSLC at 12 months to nearly quadruple that size (0.45 s.d. per s.d. of PGSLC) by age 12 years, after which effects plateaued (Fig. 4a). The PGS was also associated, albeit less strongly, with height in early childhood with effects increasing until age 12 years, after which they returned to zero by mid-adolescence, suggesting that genetic predisposition for higher BMI early in life promotes increased body size in general, including postnatal linear growth, but that this early growth does not translate into differences in height after puberty (Extended Data Fig. 5). This is in line with childhood overweight and obesity’s known associations with earlier pubertal timing30. Over time, BMI in children with a higher genetic predisposition (PGS ≥10th percentile) increased at a faster rate than those with a lower genetic predisposition, most evident after age 2.5 years (Methods, Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 13). Both boys and girls with a very early age of adiposity rebound (≤43 months), a well-established predictor of future obesity

risk31, had a higher mean PGS than those with later ages of adiposity rebound (Supplementary Table 14). We then examined whether the PGS adds predictive value over and above clinically available predictors of obesity. When added to predictors that are measurable at birth (birthweight, maternal education, pre-pregnancy maternal BMI, maternal age at date of birth and household social status), the PGS showed no clear added value for predicting ponderal index at birth or BMI at ages 3 years and 5 years (Methods and Fig. 4c, left panel). However, for predicting BMI at later ages (8, 11 and 15 years), the contribution of the predictors at birth plateaued, whereas inclusion of the PGS roughly doubled the total explained variance from 11% to 21% at age 8 and from 13% to 26% at age 15 (Fig. 4c, left panel). For the prediction of BMI in early adulthood, the contribution of the PGS especially shines through in the first few years after birth. BMI measured at age 8 explained 44% of the variation in BMI at age 18, and adding the PGS to the prediction model only raised this to 49%. In contrast, at younger ages, adding the PGS to measured BMI led to larger relative increases in the explained variance for BMI at 18 years, from 1.5-fold at age 5 (from 22% to 35%) to more than three-fold (from 8% to 26%) at 1 year of age (Fig. 4c, right panel, and Supplementary Table 15).

Response to ILIs Lifestyle modification remains a cornerstone of weight management, with multicomponent ILIs having shown success in achieving clinically relevant weight loss33. However, ILIs require substantial, sustained investment from both healthcare providers and patients, with large variation in weight loss and unintentional weight regain being common34–36. To examine whether polygenic predisposition to obesity might modify the effectiveness of such interventions, we examined whether the PGS was associated with weight loss during the first year of an ILI, and with weight regain thereafter, in two randomized controlled trials with similar intervention arms aimed at achieving 7% weight loss: the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP33) and the Look AHEAD (Action for Health in Diabetes37) studies (Methods). Among 3,909 participants (Supplementary Table 4), individuals with a higher PGSLC lost more weight during the first year in response to the ILI compared to the control group (−0.55 kg per s.d. in PGS, 95% confidence interval: −0.94 to −0.16) (Fig. 6), when adjusting for starting weight. In addition, among those who lost at least 3% of their baseline weight during the first year, a higher PGS was associated with more weight regain in the following years (up to 3 years) (0.48 kg per PGS s.d., 95% confidence interval: 0.00–0.95) (Fig. 6). These findings were directionally consistent across (self-)reported population groups.

Discussion We used GWAS summary statistics from the GIANT consortium and 23andMe, encompassing over 5.1 million people, to create ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry PGSs capturing genetic

predisposition to weight gain and obesity. Our multi-ancestry PGS more than doubled the explained variance for BMI compared to the widely used PGS by Khera et al.12. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential added value of the PGS in two distinct clinical applications: predicting adult BMI at an early age and weight change in response to ILIs. Across diverse populations, the increases in explained variance for BMI were accompanied by substantial improvements in effect sizes and discrimination metrics for obesity, with the PGSs’ standalone AUC nearing 0.80 for severe obesity. Consistent with other polygenic traits, our results underscore the importance of training sample size in driving PGS performance improvements. Nonetheless, our results also show diminishing returns of sample size increases, as has been observed for other polygenic traits38, with a 15-fold increase in total sample size (compared to PGSKhera, ~10-fold in EUR alone) leading to a 2–3-fold increase in prediction accuracy. We leveraged PRS-CSx’s unique ability to integrate GWAS summary statistics from all five broad ancestry population groups from the meta-analyses from GIANT and 23andMe17. However, recent Bayesian methods have shown promising results with smaller sample sizes by including additional variants and functional annotation, meriting consideration for future comparisons39,40. Although our results highlight the value of multi-ancestry PGS to increase PGS performance, a considerable performance gap persists for populations with substantial African-like genetic ancestry compared to other populations. This discrepancy is likely due to the underrepresentation of individuals with African-like ancestry in the training GWAS, particularly from continental Africa41, and differences in minor allele frequency (MAF) and linkage disequilibrium (LD) patterns42,43. The lower performance of the PGS in the GPC-UGR is in line with those seen therein for PGSs for other traits and the limited transferability of PGS performance between African ancestry populations, reflecting genetic and environmental differences as well as their interactions22,44–47, emphasising that much remains to be done to improve the performance of genetic risk prediction across the genetically diverse populations within Africa. For example, it remains unclear whether a finer classification of broad ancestry groups in GWAS meta-analyses and PGS development could improve downstream PGS generalizability, especially given the dominant role of GWAS sample size. For example, establishing a standardized ancestry threshold14,48 may improve the accuracy of population-specific risk stratification and ensure that the score is returned only in populations where it meets an acceptable performance threshold. Within ALSPAC, the PGS—which was developed for adult BMI— already shows an effect on BMI early in life. Effect sizes rapidly increased with age and were accompanied by clear divergence of BMI trajectories throughout childhood and adolescence. As a result, the PGS showed added value beyond clinically available predictors assessed at birth for predicting BMI measured after age 5. This is in line with previous research on the dynamic relationship between genetic variation and adiposity in early life12,49,50. Particularly elucidating are the observations from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) with repeated measurements across narrow age windows51. They show that BMI has a rapidly changing genetic architecture during the first 8 years of life with a ‘late rise’ cluster of variants, emerging in late childhood, which show limited association before the adiposity rebound but have persistent effects on BMI into adult life51. This also explains why our PGS shows its value for predicting adult BMI during the earliest years of life, up to age 5, when measured BMI has limited value as a predictor. With a growing number of obesity prevention trials commencing in early life52,53, our results provide important context at what age(s) PGSs for obesity, potentially in tandem with PGSs of obesity-related complications, could be considered promising candidate predictors to help guide risk stratification and the implementation of such interventions. In the PLCO study, a higher PGS was associated with weight gain over a 30-year period from early adulthood to midlife. Additionally, for individuals aged 20, knowing their PGS modestly improved the prediction of obesity at age 50, more so for those without overweight or obesity at age 20. This suggests that particularly individuals with an early adulthood BMI below their genetically predicted BMI are at risk of gaining weight to match their innate predisposition. Our findings are consistent with those from the CARDIA study54, showing that PGSs for obesity only marginally improve the prediction of midlife BMI when combined with early adulthood BMI measurements, contrasting with its predictive value in early life. Analyzing clinical trial data of ILIs, we observed that individuals with a higher PGS lost modestly more weight during the first year. However, this group was also at higher risk of weight regain after this most intensive portion of the intervention had concluded. This may seem counterintuitive to the expectation that those with a higher genetic risk will benefit less from weight loss interventions. However, this observation is supported by a strong body of literature reporting that those most genetically predisposed to obesity are also those most responsive to changes in an obesogenic environment55–63. However, the literature on the role of genetics modifying response to weight loss interventions remains sparse and ambiguous, reflecting differences in variants considered, methods and study design, highlighting the need for well-powered PGSs64–73. It will be of interest to investigate whether PGSs for obesity have predictive utility for the fast-growing arsenal of pharmacotherapies aimed at weight loss. Separately, the current results offer crucial context when conveying genetic results of obesity risk to participants, which has generally shown either no or even short-lived adverse effects on risk-reducing behavior74–77. Rather, our findings emphasize that individuals with a high genetic predisposition to obesity may respond more to lifestyle changes and, thus, contrast with the determinist view that genetic predisposition is unmodifiable78. This is further reinforced by evidence that polygenic susceptibility can mitigate or exacerbate the impact of pathogenic variants in MC4R, underscoring the complexity of genetic influences on obesity79. We look forward to the findings of the Electronic MEdical Records and GEnomics (eMERGE) network’s PGS-based genome-informed risk assessment being returned to 25,000 diverse adults and children for 11 conditions, including obesity/BMI14.

Taken together, we show that BMI PGSs can be used for prediction of adult obesity throughout the life course, particularly in early life, and for severe obesity. This PGS represents a substantial improvement compared to previous scores and may help to identify individuals at high risk to allow for timely prevention or treatment of obesity, such as through integration in a broader predictive framework jointly modeling genetic and environmental risk.

Methods Study populations The list of studies contributing to the GWAS meta-analyses for BMI, which served as the training data for the presented PGSs, is provided in Supplementary Table 1. The study populations described below are those that contributed as a PGS tuning or validation population. The UKBB is a prospective cohort study that enrolled approximately 500,000 people from across the UK, aged 40–69 years at recruitment, between 2006 and 2010 (ref. 18). At recruitment, participants completed detailed questionnaires, underwent a range of physical measures and provided blood, urine and saliva samples. BMI was calculated using height (measured in whole centimeters) and weight (to the nearest 0.1 kg). Females who were pregnant at the time of assessment were excluded from our analysis. As a measure of comparative childhood body size, participants were asked: ‘When you were 10 years old, compared to average, would you describe yourself as: (i) thinner, (ii) plumper, (iii) about average?’. The MVP has recruited over 1 million people from Veteran Affairs (VA) Medical Centers across the United States since 2011 (ref. 19). Veterans who volunteer provide a blood sample for biobanking, complete baseline and lifestyle questionnaires and consent to allow access to clinical data from VA electronic health records (EHRs). For the current study, PGS performance was assessed in the MVP’s third release of genomic data (R3) using additional participants without overlap, with earlier data releases contributing to the GIANT GWAS meta-analyses. Phenotypic and genomic data related to the association analysis of BMI were previously described20. The Institute for Personalized Medicine BioMe Biobank, founded in 2007, is an ancestrally and culturally highly diverse EHR-linked biorepository enrolling participants non-selectively from across the Mount Sinai Health System in New York City21. At enrollment, participants consent to link their DNA and plasma samples to deidentified EHRs. The clinical and EHR information is complemented by a baseline questionnaire that gathers demographic and lifestyle information. BMI was calculated using weight and height from baseline and outpatient EHR measurements, using median height and weight measured at or within 60 days before/after the enrollment visit, after several cleaning steps (Supplementary Table 3). The GPC-UGR is a population-based open cohort study established in 1989 by the Medical Research Council (UK) in collaboration with the Uganda Virus Research Institute (UVRI) to monitor the HIV epidemic and its determinants in neighboring villages in rural southwestern Uganda, in the Kyamulibwa subcounty of the Kalungu district, approximately 120 km from Entebbe town. Since 2010, its mandate has expanded to incorporate the epidemiology and genetics of both communicable and non-communicable diseases22. The GPC-UGR was initially recruited and assessed through annual house-to-house census and survey rounds until 2012, when biannual surveys commenced. For the current study, we included individuals aged 18 years and older who have been either whole-genome genotyped or whole-genome sequenced80,81. The ALSPAC is a prospective birth cohort from the southwest of England established to investigate environmental and genetic characteristics that influence health, development and growth of children and their parents27–29. Full details of the cohort and study design are available at http://www.alspac.bris.ac.uk. In brief, pregnant females residing in Avon, UK, with expected dates of delivery between 1 April 1991 and 31 December 1992 were invited to take part in the study. The initial number of pregnancies enrolled was 14,541, with 13,988 children who were alive at 1 year of age. The children resulting from these pregnancies have been followed-up to date with measures obtained through regular questionnaires and clinical visits, providing information on a range of behavioral, lifestyle and biological data. More specifically, a 10% sample of the ALSPAC cohort, known as the Children in Focus (CiF) group, attended clinics at the University of Bristol at various time

intervals between 4 months and 61 months of age, whereas the entire ALSPAC cohort was invited to attend regular research clinics from age 7. When the oldest children were approximately age 7, an attempt was made to bolster the initial sample with eligible individuals who had failed to join the study originally. The total sample size available for analyses using any data collected after the age of 7 is, therefore, 15,447 pregnancies, with 14,901 children who were alive at 1 year of age. Study data were collected and managed using Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) tools hosted at the University of Bristol82. REDCap is a secure, web-based software platform designed to support data capture for research studies. Details on sample selection for the current analyses are presented in Supplementary Table 3. Please note that the study website contains details of all data that are available through a fully searchable data dictionary and variable search tool (http://www. bristol.ac.uk/alspac/researchers/our-data/). The PLCO Cancer Screening Trial was a multicenter randomized controlled trial in the United States that enrolled males and females aged 55–74 years from 1993 to 2001 to evaluate the effectiveness of different screening programs on cancer mortality32. In the baseline questionnaire, participants self-reported their weight at age 20 years, age 50 years and baseline as well as their height. For the current study, we restricted the analyses to genotyped participants who had not contributed to the underlying GWAS meta-analyses and had information available on their weight and BMI at both age 20 and age 50. The DPP was a 27-site parallel-arm randomized controlled trial designed to determine whether either the oral diabetes drug metformin or an ILI (primarily fat gram, calorie and physical activity goals) aimed at approximately 7% weight loss, compared to inactive tablets and standard lifestyle recommendations, could prevent or delay type 2 diabetes onset in ethnically diverse high-risk individuals with prediabetes and overweight or obesity33. For the current study, we excluded individuals from the metformin arm as well as those from a fourth intervention arm, troglitazone, which was discontinued at an early stage. Moreover, we focused on the individuals comprising the three largest race and ethnicity categories (White, Black and Hispanic, as reported by database of Genotypes and Phenotypes (dbGAP) variable phv00201855.v2.p1) who had consented to being genotyped. Look AHEAD was a 16-site parallel-arm randomized controlled trial that assessed the long-term effects of an ILI in ethnically diverse patients with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes on cardiovascular morbidity and mortality37. The lifestyle intervention was modeled after the DPP lifestyle intervention and similarly aimed at 7% weight loss but with more ambitious individual goals for several intervention components83. Although those in both trial arms were provided one session of education on diabetes and cardiovascular risk at baseline, the comparison arm thereafter received the option of attending only three sessions per year on nutrition, physical activity and social support, with no explicit weight loss goals. As for the DPP, we restricted our analyses to genotyped participants who self-reported as being of African American/Black, Hispanic and White race and ethnicity on the baseline questionnaire. Population descriptors and study-provided population labels and genotyping, phenotyping and participant characteristics are presented in Supplementary Tables 3 and 4. No new data (that is, measurements) were collected for this study, and no participant compensation was provided for the analyses conducted. PGS construction and tuning To derive our scores, we used summary statistics from the ongoing GWAS meta-analyses for BMI conducted by the GIANT consortium (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/collaboration/giant/index.php/ GIANT_consortium) in collaboration with 23andMe. Prior to each GWAS, BMI (kg m−2) underwent rank-based inverse-normal transformation by sex, similarity to major ancestry group (AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR, SAS) and case–control status as appropriate, with age, age2, principal components of population structure and study-specific covariates regressed out. Ancestry group assignment was defined independently by each contributing study, as previously described84. Additive GWAS analyses were performed primarily using RVTESTS for 1000 Genomes Project (1000G) phase 3 or Haplotype Reference Consortium (HRC)-imputed data85. For 23andMe, which performed its GWAS on BMI using self-reported height and weight, see Supplementary Table 2 for details on phenotyping, ancestry group assignment and GWAS methodology. Quality control of the study-specific files was conducted using EasyQC86, followed by fixed-effect meta-analysis by ancestry group using RAREMETAL87. When performing the GWAS meta-analyses to train the PGSs with, we purposely excluded data from several populations (ALSPAC, BioMe and UKBB). No additional genomic control was applied to the resulting summary statistics. For PGS derivation, we employed PRS-CS and its multi-ancestral extension PRS-CSx (versions 1.0.0)16,17. In short, PRS-CS(x) uses a Bayesian regression framework and assumes a continuous shrinkage prior on single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) effects. Whereas PRS-CS focuses on creating ancestry-specific scores, informed only by the GWAS summary statistics and LD information of a given population, PRS-CSx uses a shared prior to couple SNP effects across populations and explicitly models population-specific allele frequencies and LD patterns to create multi-ancestry scores. Both methods were implemented using the software’s default settings (that is, gamma–gamma priors set to a = 1 and b = 0.5, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) total and burn-in iterations set at 1,000 times and 500 times the number of discovery populations and MC thinning factor set at 5), with input being ancestry-matched summary statistics and PRS-CS(x) developer-provided 1000G LD reference panels of common HapMap3 variants (AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR, SAS). PRS-CS(x) uses a global scaling parameter (Φ), which requires tuning. In addition to small-scale grid testing of Φ (1 × 10−6, 1 × 10−4, 1 × 10−2, 1), we ran PRS-CS(x) using its ‘auto’ option, which learns Φ automatically from the GWAS summary statistics. Finally, PRS-CSx was performed separately using its default ‘linear combination’ as well as its ‘meta’ version. In the first, a set of population-specific PGSs is outputted (that is, five in our case), for which the optimal linear combination needs to be derived for each target population (for example, AFR) in a population-matched tuning dataset. For ‘meta’, the population-specific posterior SNP effects

are integrated using an inverse-variance weighted meta-analysis in the Gibbs sampler, producing a single score that can theoretically be applied regardless of the target population. The variants considered for PGS derivation were those present in the 1000G reference panels mentioned above (HapMap3 variants (n = 1–1.2 million across panels), which were common in 1000G populations, excluding ambiguous A/T or G/C variants), which additionally had an INFO > 0.3 (that is, imputation quality) in the overall UKBB. Ancestry-specific summary statistics were further restricted to the variants with a variant-specific sample size of at least a third of the maximum sample size for that ancestry. Tuning of Φ and derivation of PRS-CSx’s linear combination weights were performed in the same subsets of the UKBB. More specifically, we used genetically determined relatedness and ancestry assignments provided by the Pan-UKBB Team (https://pan.ukbb.broadinstitute.org, UKBB return 2442) to subset the UKBB into groups of unrelated individuals of African-like, Admixed American-like, Central/South Asian-like, East Asian-like, European-like (random subset of 20,000 individuals) and Middle Eastern-like ancestry. The target-population-specific (for example, AFR) linear combination weights for PRS-CSx (for each Φ) were derived from a joint linear regression model of rank-based inverse-normal transformed BMI (by sex and population) on the five population-specific scores (each standardized to mean zero and unit variance in the corresponding tuning dataset—for example, UKBBAFR), age, 10 principal components and genotyping array. Explained variance for BMI was defined as the incremental adjusted R2 from linear regression for rank-based inverse-normal transformed BMI (by sex and population), when adding the PGS predictor to a model containing age, principal components and genotyping array. Confidence intervals (95%) were determined using bootstrapping with 1,000 repetitions. As comparator, we created a score of quasi-independent associations after performing approximate conditional and joint (COJO) multiple-SNP analysis88, as implemented in GCTA89, using the results from the multi-ancestral GWAS summary statistics when leaving out only the UKBB. We used genotypes from a previously described set of 50,000 unrelated UKBBEUR participants84 as our LD reference panel for GCTA-COJO, with parameters set to: –diff-freq 0.1; –maf 0.01; –cojo-collinear 0.9; –cojo-p 5 × 10−9. The scores with the highest explained variance across multiple tuning population datasets (PRS-CSx linear combination and meta versions, with Φ 1 × 10−2) were then taken forward to the validation populations, which performed study-level variant filtering on imputation quality when constructing each PGS (Supplementary Table 3). The results of PGSmeta are presented throughout the supplementary tables. Of note, in August 2023, a new version of PRS-CSx was released (version 1.1.0) to address potential reductions in performance due to truncating of GWAS summary statistics P values below 1 × 10−323. Given our inclusion of several variants with P values below this threshold (among the PGS variants: n = 154 for EUR, n = 12 for AMR), we reran PRS-CSx with Φ 1 × 10−2 but did not observe markedly different results in PGS performance within the UKBB tuning populations (Supplementary Table 18).

Confidence intervals (95%) were calculated using bootstrapping with 1,000 repetitions.

The main comparator for all analyses was a previously published LDpred-derived PGS for BMI (PGSKhera)12, which was based on the results from a GIANT consortium GWAS meta-analysis including up to 339,224 individuals of primarily European ancestry24. We chose PGSKhera as our comparator as it is the most widely recognized and extensively used PGS for BMI within the obesity research community, thereby serving as a well-established benchmark.

Tail comparisons after ancestry correction Due to on-average differences in LD structure and allele frequencies, the distribution of a PGS (for example, mean and variance) can differ across ancestral populations. This was also observed for the five population-specific PGSs that were linearly combined to create PGSLC (Extended Data Fig. 4). As performance metrics that rely on thresholding the PGS distribution (for example, top 10%) may be impacted by such on-average differences90, particularly in admixed populations, we modeled the mean and variance of the population-specific PGSs through principal component analysis of the 1000G reference panel. For this, we applied a correction described by the eMERGE network14,91, which represents a modified version of the approach by Khera et al.92. Starting with a publicly available, curated version of the 1000G reference panel (https://broadinstitute.github.io/warp/ docs/Pipelines/Imputation_Pipeline/references_overview; gs:// broad-gotc-test-storage/imputation/1000 G_reference_panel), we first excluded variants with MAF < 1% across 1000G superpopulations, before determining the overlap with genotyped variants available for both the UKBB and BioMe.
