Multi-ancestry PGS trained only with GIANT consortium data Although we primarily report on the development and performance of the PGSLC trained with the larger GIANT+23andMe BMI GWAS meta-analyses results, we initially developed a multi-ancestry PGS with the GIANT-only results. For this, we used PRS-CS, combining GIANT’s combined multi-ancestral GWAS summary statistics (including BioMe but excluding the UKBB and the ALSPAC study) with a previously described multi-ancestry 1000G-based LD reference panel created following the same protocol as described by the PRS-CS authors94. We restricted variants to those present in the LD reference panel, which additionally had MAF ≥ 0.1% and INFO ≥ 0.8 in the overall UKBB, resulting in a total of 1,217,710 variants included. We did not specify a genome-wide shrinkage parameter for PRS-CS, which it therefore learned from the training data using a fully Bayesian approach (its ‘auto’ option). In collaboration with the eMERGE network, this GIANT-only PGS was included among a select group of trait-specific scores currently being returned as part of a genome-informed risk assessment (GIRA) to 25,000 diverse adults and children and their healthcare providers in an ongoing prospective cohort study across 10 clinical sites, as recently described14,48. In line with the aim of returning a high-risk versus a not-high-risk GIRA status to participants, we estimated the odds ratio for obesity class I (or higher) for being in the top 3% of the PGS distribution (versus bottom 97%) within the subset of BioMe participants genotyped with the Global Screening Array (with 1000G imputation) who had not contributed to the underlying GIANT GWAS meta-analysis nor were related to those who did. Accounting for age, sex and four principal components, we observed that values within the top 3% of this PGS were associated with 4.08 (95% confidence interval: 3.02–5.52) times as high odds for prevalent obesity in individuals of self-reported European descent, with 2.54 (95% confidence interval: 1.55–3.98) for individuals of self-reported African descent, with 2.33 (95% confidence interval: 1.64–3.31) for individuals of self-reported Hispanic/Latino descent and with 5.73 (95% confidence interval: 2.28–14.57) for individuals of self-reported Asian descent. The weights for this GIANT-only PGS are made available through the PGS Catalog alongside the weights for PGSLC and PGSmeta (see ‘Data availability’).

Childhood and adolescence Within the ALSPAC study, repeated anthropometric measurements are available from birth to age 24. We employed both cross-sectional and multilevel analyses to provide complementary perspectives: cross-sectional analyses facilitate granular comparisons at each timepoint, whereas multilevel models capture longitudinal trajectories and population-level divergence over time. First, we assessed repeated cross-sectional associations between the standardized PGS (PGSLC using linear combination weights from UKBBEUR) and all available measures of BMI (or ponderal index at birth) and height. Anthropometric measurements were rank-based inverse-normal transformed separately by sex, at each timepoint, and analyses were adjusted for age at timepoint and principal components. Longitudinal analyses using linear spline multilevel models were conducted to examine the association between the PGS (bottom 10%, middle 80%, top 10%) and change in untransformed BMI and height between 4 months and 24 years. Multilevel models estimate the mean trajectories of each anthropometric trait while accounting for non-independence of repeated measures within individuals, change in scale and variance of measures over time and differences in the number and timing of measurements between individuals (using all available data from all eligible participants under a missing-at-random assumption). Linear splines allow knot points to be fitted at different ages to derive periods of change that are approximately linear. All participants with at least one measure of the anthropometric traits were included under a missing-at-random assumption to minimize selection bias in trajectories estimated using linear spline multilevel models (with two levels of random effects: measurement occasion (that is, age to the nearest integer in years) and individual), allowing individuals to have different intercepts and slopes and, thus, their own trajectories. Knot points were placed as follows for each anthropometric trait based on the distribution and longitudinal pattern of measures between the earliest measure and 24 years: at ages 4 months and 8 months and at ages 2.5 years, 5 years, 8 years and 15 years for BMI and at ages 1 year, 5 years and 15 years for height. Interaction terms between PGS and each spline were included in the models to estimate the difference in the intercepts (earliest anthropometric trait measurement) and slopes (change in anthropometric trait from the earliest measure to 24 years) between the three PGS categories. Additionally, interaction terms between sex and the first 10 genetic principal components with each spline were included to estimate the difference in intercepts and slopes between males and females; therefore, models were adjusted for sex and principal components. All longitudinal models were created in MLwiN version 3.04 called from Stata version 15 using the ‘runmlwin’ command95. In the CiF subset of the cohort, age at adiposity rebound was available, categorized as very early (at/before 43 months), early (from 49 months but before 61 months) and later (after 61 months)96. These children represent a 10% sample of the cohort, randomly selected for more detailed investigations, and are representative of the entire cohort (https://www.bristol.ac.uk/alspac/researchers/cohort-profile/). One-way ANOVA was used to test for differences in mean PGS across categories, in boys and girls separately and combined. Added value of the PGS for prediction of BMI (rank-based inversenormal transformed by sex) at given timepoints was quantified as incremental explained variance, when adding the PGS to different sets of predictors. First, we examined R2 for BMI at birth and at 3, 5, 8, 11 and 15 years, when adding the PGS to a model containing multiple relatively easily obtainable clinical variables that would be available at birth (birthweight, maternal education, pre-pregnancy maternal BMI, maternal age at date of birth and household social status). Details regarding phenotyping of these variables can be found in Supplementary Table 3. Separately, for R2 for BMI at age 18, we added the PGS to separate models containing BMI from a given early-life timepoint (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 years). Confidence intervals (95%) were calculated using bootstrapping with 1,000 repetitions.

From early adulthood to middle age Within PLCO, we assessed the population-statified and sex-stratified association between the standardized PGSLC (using linear combination weights from the UKBB most closely corresponding to each testing population) and per-5-year change between ages 20 and 50 in weight and BMI, with and without adjustment for the initial measurement at age 20. These analyses were additionally adjusted for birth year, sex (where appropriate) and principal components. We calculated the population-stratified AUC of the PGS for obesity outcomes at age 50. For this, we ran models including (i) birth year and sex, (ii) birth year, sex, principal components and PGSLC, (iii) birth year, sex, principal components and BMI at age 20 and (iv) birth year, sex, principal components, BMI at age 20 and PGSLC. We separately ran model (iv) when including an interaction term between the PGS and BMI at age 20. Based on evidence for statistical interaction between the PGS and BMI at age 20 for predicting obesity at age 50 across multiple populations (Supplementary Table 16), we stratified our analyses on the presence of overweight or obesity at age 20 and, additionally, on sex. Confidence intervals (95%) for AUC were calculated using DeLong’s method.

PGS and weight change due to ILIs Although neither intervention nor comparison arms were identical across DPP and Look AHEAD, both intervention arms were aimed at 7% weight loss while focused on the same process features83, and both represent a large shift in lifestyle behavior relative to the comparison arms. As such, we decided to pool study-specific effect estimates via inverse-variance weighted meta-analysis. In each study, we ran analyses after pooling the three largest population groups present in both trials: Black and/or African American, Hispanic and White (Supplementary Table 3). Population-stratified analyses were separately run as well. Within each study-specific population, we applied the linear combination weights for PGSLC most closely aligned with the target population (AFR, AMR and EUR, respectively). These scores were then standardized within the matching population, ignoring trial arm, whereafter we standardized again across all individuals for the population-pooled analyses. Due to restricting analyses to genotyped individuals from the three largest population groups, trial randomization was, by definition, broken. To investigate potential shifts in the PGS, we plotted its distribution by trial arm, which showed minimal shifts in distribution (Extended Data Fig. 7). To investigate weight change, we focused on annual weight measurements. The weight loss nadir in both trials is known to occur at the 1-year mark, after which many individuals start regaining weight. As such, we separately examined the association of the PGS with (i) weight at year 1 (adjusting for baseline weight) and (ii) repeated weight measurements beyond year 1 up to year 4 (adjusting for weight at year 1) in the subset of individuals who had lost ≥3% of their initial body weight in the first year. Analyses were run by trial arm using linear mixed models with random intercepts, with additional covariates being age, sex, principal components, the initial weight measurement (baseline or year 1) and random slopes for time (years). In addition, we ran trial–arm combined models in which we examined interaction effects between trial arm and PGS. These interaction terms are our main estimates of interest, as they reflect how genetic predisposition to obesity modifies the intervention’s effect on weight change, relative to the comparison arm. Study-specific main and interaction effect estimates were separately pooled by means of inverse-variance weighted fixed-effect meta-analysis. Participant characteristics are presented in Supplementary Table 4.

# SEEK-VEC: Robust Latent Structure Discovery via Ensemble Topic Modeling

**Authors:** Rebecca Danning; Zheng Tracy Ke; Rong Ma; Xihong Lin

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Biostatistics, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health | 2Department of Statistics, Harvard University

## Abstract

Count data are ubiquitous across many applications in which understanding hidden patterns, or latent structure, is of interest. Topic modeling is a powerful tool for detecting latent structure in count data. However, standard topic modeling methods are often constrained by their restrictive assumptions, susceptible to noise, and sensitive to misspecification of the number of topics, which is particularly of concern when analyzing non-text data. Here, we introduce SEEK-VEC (Spectral Ensembling of topic models with Eigenscore for K-agnostic Vocabulary Embedding and Classification), an ensemble framework for count data that integrates insights from multiple candidate topic models through a spectral ensembling procedure. This approach automatically reinforces signal and mitigates noise to generate a consensus low-dimensional embedding of the data. SEEK-VEC produces prioritization scores and grouping scores that enable variable classification, interactive pattern discovery, and model diagnostics. Through simulations, we demonstrate that SEEK-VEC is robust under realistic settings and outperforms state-of-the-art oracle methods, particularly when signal strength is weak. Applied to diverse real-world datasets, including self-reported psychopathology symptom data, food preference questionnaires, and single-cell transcriptomics, SEEK-VEC reveals latent structures that provide scientifically meaningful insights.

## Introduction

Topic modeling is a statistical approach in text analysis that aims to identify a small set of topics underlying a large collection of documents [1]. This can be thought of as a dimensionality reduction procedure, as it aims to summarize the entire vocabulary with respect to a space defined by the latent topics. Topic modeling typically operates on integer data representing counts of words per document, but can also be used in non-text integer data settings. In particular, topic modeling has been used in on a wide variety of biomedical data, such as microarrays [2], genome annotation [3], and MRI data [4]. The “topics” found from biomedical data represent latent biological concepts that can yield insight into underlying structure [5]. Additionally, the output of a topic model can be used to separate signal-relevant words from uninformative words [6]. This is particularly useful in non-text applications where there is an absence of a conventional notion of “vocabulary”, as one can benefit from utilizing the identified signal-relevant words for downstream tasks such as survey design, construct validation, and biological modeling.

However, when applied to non-text data, standard topic modeling approaches face significant challenges, both in their underlying assumptions and in practical implementations. First, many topic modeling methods rely on an “anchor word” assumption, or separability assumption, to ensure model identifiability [7, 8]. The basic idea is that for each topic, there is at least one word–an anchor word–that identifies the topic, meaning that it appears exclusively in one topic and not others [1, 9]. While this condition is commonly satisfied in text data with large numbers of anchor words per topic [10], it is often not the case for non-text applications. For example, statistical analysis of the transcripts from meetings of the Federal Open Market Committee discussing monetary policy strategy rejected the null hypothesis that the corpus contained anchor words [11]. As such, standard topic modeling algorithms may underperform in non-text applications. Second, most existing topic modeling methods require specifying the number of topics K in advance for implementation [10, 12–14]. But consistently estimating K from the data remains a challenging task in real-world applications [10]. Several data-driven approaches have been developed for estimating K , include analyzing the singular values of the data [15], perplexity-based cross-validation techniques [16], and model-fitting criteria such as BIC [17], yet so far there is no consensus on their relative performance and reliability in different applications. Alternatively, K can be chosen in part due to the interpretability of the topics based on subject-matter expertise [1], but this leaves the model open to subjectivity bias, and may not be feasible in many non-text applications. Importantly, as we will show below, inaccurate estimation of K can yield misleading results and even false conclusions about the data.

To address these limitations, in this paper we present SEEK-VEC (Spectral Ensembling of topic models with Eigenscore for K-agnostic Vocabulary Embedding and Classification), an ensemble machine learning method for characterizing latent structure in count data. SEEK-VEC outperforms existing methods in challenging scenarios where the anchor word assumption is violated, and it does not require the number of topics to be prespecified. It leverages the performance-improving properties of ensemble learning strategies [18, 19] and is a flexible framework for enhancing any existing topic modeling algorithm. Here, we combine our ensemble approach with Topic-SCORE [1, 10], a state-of-the-art method for topic modeling that uses singular value decomposition to facilitate fast estimation of the low-rank topic matrix with theoretical guarantees. SEEK-VEC produces two complementary sets of scores. Prioritization scores distinguish important variables (or words) from less informative ones, while grouping scores quantify the strength of relationships among variables. Together, these scores enable downstream applications such as variable classification, interactive pattern discovery, and model diagnostics. Through extensive numerical simulations, we show that SEEK-VEC consistently outperforms existing topic modeling methods across various tasks under realistic noisy data conditions. We then apply SEEK-VEC to four real-world datasets, each with a nonstandard “vocabulary”, including self-reported psychopathology symptom data in adults with autism, a food preferences questionnaire from the UK Biobank, and two single-cell RNA-seq datasets. Across these applications, SEEK-VEC uncovers meaningful patterns in the data without requiring prior knowledge of the latent dimensionality. The R package implementation of SEEK-VEC is available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/rdanning/seekvec

## Results

### Overview of SEEK-VEC

SEEK-VEC builds on the topic model, a statistical framework designed for count data that aims to uncover the latent dimensions, or topics, along which the vocabulary are located. There are three main steps to the method. First, a topic model is fitted for each of a range of candidate topic counts K . Second, the output of each topic model is converted into a novel sparse representation called the joint hallmark projection matrix that captures the latent embedding information from the model without relying on K . Finally, these representations are combined into a consensus-weighted embedding using a spectral ensembling procedure. The diagonal values of this output matrix can be used to prioritize the vocabulary with respect to how much signal it contains of the underlying latent structure, and the off-diagonal values can be used to understand the grouping structure among the vocabulary. SEEK-VEC is summarized in Figure 1a, and additional details of its implementation are given in the Methods section.

*Figure 1:: (a) Overview of SEEK-VEC. In the above example, there are three candidate values of K : 𝒦 = { k 1 , k 2 , k 3 } . In step 1, topic modeling is run on the input corpus matrix for each candidate value of K to yield a collection of R p × K topic matrices. In step 2, each topic matrix is row-normalized to a topic loadings matrix and then converted into a R p × p joint hallmark projection matrix. In step 3, these joint hallmark projection matrices are ensembled using a spectral ensembling procedure. The output is the ensembled joint hallmark projection matrix O ^ ∈ R p × p . (b) Toy example demonstrating the procedure for converting a topic matrix into a joint hallmark projection matrix. The topic matrix is the direct output of a topic modeling algorithm, where each column represents a distribution on the vocabulary and sums to 1. The loadings matrix is the row-normalized version of the topic matrix. Notably, words such as “is” and “the”, which are common to all topics, have higher values in the topic matrix but relatively low values in the loadings matrix. The hallmark matrix is a dichotomized version of the loadings matrix. This represents the standard topic modeling procedure of choosing vocabulary words that are representative of each topic. The joint hallmark projection matrix is the hallmark matrix multiplied by its transpose. Words with a value of 0 along the diagonal (e.g. “is” and “the”) are not representative of any topic. Words with a 1 along the diagonal identify a single topic (e.g. “brush” for Topic 2). Words with a value of 2 along the diagonal link topics (e.g. “ball” links Topic 1 and Topic 3). The values on the off-diagonal indicate the number of topics for which two words are jointly representative. The reordered joint hallmark projection matrix demonstrates how block structure can be used to recover topics and understand meta-relationships among the topics.*

#### Step 1: Obtain a topic matrix for a range of topic counts

Topic modeling algorithms take as input a corpus matrix D ∈ R p × n , which contains the counts of each of p vocabulary words in each of n documents, and a number of topics K . Each of the n documents is thought to comprise some combination of the K topics. The output is a topic matrix A ∈ R p × K , each column of which represents a probability distribution over the p vocabulary words for each topic. Each row of A can be viewed as representing a vocabulary word’s position in K -dimensional space, with each axis corresponding to a topic. The first step of SEEK-VEC is to run a topic modeling algorithm for a collection of candidate values 𝒦 ; typically, 𝒦 is a range of consecutive values of K . This step yields a collection of candidate topic matrices A K for each K ∈ 𝒦 . SEEK-VEC implements Topic-SCORE [10] for topic modeling; a comparison of alternative topic modeling algorithms can be found in Section S1.1.

#### Step 2: Convert each topic matrix into a joint hallmark projection matrix

While the immediate output from a topic model is a p × K matrix containing the probability of each vocabulary word in each topic, in practice the row-normalized version of this matrix, denoted by B and called the topic loading matrix, is used for interpretation. The matrix B is obtained by dividing each row of A by the row sum. This matrix is preferred because it shows the relative weight of each word across the topics, and therefore allows for the interpretation of topics based on the words with the highest loadings. Typically, the representative words for each topic are extracted by choosing the words whose loadings at this topic are above a certain threshold. This is equivalent to dichotomizing the topic loading matrix B to a hallmark matrix H ∈ R p × k whose entries only take binary values. We consider the joint hallmark projection matrix O = H H ⊤ as a pairwise distance matrix for vocabulary words. Notably, O is a p × p matrix, and thus summarizes information from the K -dimensional word embeddings in a form that is free of K .

The joint hallmark projection matrix provides a valuable lens into the relationships among the vocabulary words as well as among the topics. Thinking of H as a bipartite graph representing edges between topics and words, O is equivalent to the one-mode projection network of that graph [20]. The values along the diagonal of O indicate the number of topics for which a word is representative. More generally, this is the number of latent dimensions for which the word contains strong signal. Words with a diagonal value of 1 are only representative for a single topic, and therefore can be used to identify a topic. Words with a diagonal value greater than 1 are meta-informative: these words are representative for more than one topic and therefore indicate a relationship among topics with respect to the vocabulary. Words with a diagonal value of 0 can be disregarded when interpreting the topics. The values on the off-diagonal are also interpretable: the value O i j represents the number of topics for which word i and word j are both representative, so O i j > 0 indicates a relationship among words with respect to the topics. An example of this procedure is shown in Figure 1b.

#### Step 3: Ensemble the joint hallmark projection matrices with eigenscore

Each joint hallmark projection matrix represents an embedding of the vocabulary in potentially-misspecified K -dimensional space. As such, each embedding may contain both signal and noise with respect to the true underlying latent structure. Therefore, we can combine the insights from each model in a way that upweights consensus signal and downweights individual noise. This is done using a spectral ensembling method adapted from the eigenscore [21] method, which is described in further detail in the Methods section. The output of this method is the ensembled joint hallmark projection matrix O ^ ∈ R p × p that represents a consensus embedding of the vocabulary.

The matrix O ^ yields key information about the vocabulary and its underlying structure: the diagonal values of the matrix contain prioritization scores, which estimate the signal contained in each vocabulary word. These scores can be used to filter the vocabulary: words with zero or near-zero scores likely are uninformative with respect to any latent structure (e.g. “the” in Figure 1b), whereas words with high scores should be prioritized for downstream analysis. The off-diagonal values of the matrix contain grouping scores, where a high grouping score between two words indicates shared signal with respect to the latent structure (e.g. “bat” and “ball” in Figure 1b) and therefore indicate group structure that should be considered in downstream analysis and interpretation.

### Advantages of SEEK-VEC and Simulation Results

To test the ability of SEEK-VEC to estimate the true prioritization and grouping scores, we compare SEEK-VEC, ensembling K = 3 to K = 12 , to each of the component Topic-SCORE matrices. In these scenarios, we simulate a vocabulary of p = 2000 words across K = 6 topics in n = 1000 documents of length N = 5000 . We simulate 10% of the vocabulary words as identifying words (representative for one randomly-selected topic) and simulate 20% of the words as metainformative words (representative for two randomly-selected topics). In the strong-anchor setting, the representative words have loadings that are 10× that of the remaining topics. In the weak-anchor setting, the representative words have loadings that are 3× that of the remaining topics. Results for varying degrees of weakened signal strength are shown in the supplement. In both settings, the remaining 70% uninformative have equal loadings across all topics. Example rows from the simulated loadings matrices are shown in Figure 2a. The data are simulated under the word frequency heterogeneity setting. In this setting, there is a severe discrepancy in the overall frequency of the vocabulary words, which is common in realistic text settings and is known as Zipf’s Law [22]. We dichotomize the topic loadings matrix by selecting the top t = 0.3 proportion of words; extended results for other threshold values are shown in Section S1.2.

*Figure 2:: (a) Median cumulative runtimes of the ensembling procedure compared to running the standard topic models for four topic modeling methods. Columns represent different values of p . The green lines show the cumulative runtimes of running the base topic model for K = { 3 , … , X } , where X is the x -axis value. The other lines show the additional time taken to ensemble these models with varying values of the threshold t . (b) Example rows of from the loadings matrix in the Strong and Weak conditions for each of the three categories of words. (c) Performance of the estimated prioritization scores, which measure how relevant each word is to the underlying latent structure. The y-axis shows the correlations across simulations with the true prioritization scores. (d) AUCs assessing the performance of each matrix’s prioritization scores for separating informative words from uninformative words. (e) Performance of the of the estimated grouping scores, which measure how closely-related two words are with respect to the underlying latent structure. The y-axis shows the correlations across simulations with the true grouping scores.*

#### SEEK-VEC more reliably differentiates representative words from uninformative words

The diagonal of the true joint hallmark projection matrix is equal to the number of topics for which a given word is representative and can be treated as a prioritization score, where words that have higher prioritization scores contain more information about the underlying topic structure. Words that are uninformative, therefore, have a prioritization score of 0, while identifying words have a true prioritization score of 1 and metainformative words have a true prioritization score greater than 1. Figure 2b shows the correlations between the estimated prioritization scores derived from the standard and ensemble models with the true prioritization scores. For the standard Topic-SCORE model, the under- and correctly-specified models (K3 to K6) yield a moderately strong positive correlation with the true prioritization scores. The over-specified models, however, have a correlation close to zero. Under the strong anchor condition in the top row, SEEK-VEC is slightly worse than the oracle Topic-SCORE model, but better than any misspecified model.

The bottom row of Figure 2b shows the correlations under weak-anchor simulation settings. In this setting, the loadings for the representative words of a topic become more similar to the loadings of those words on topics for which they are not representative. This presents a strong violation to the separability or anchor word condition that is typically required for topic models to be identifiable [7, 10]. The effects of the violation of this assumption are clearly shown by the performance of standard Topic-SCORE; unlike under the strong-anchor setting, the oracle model fails to capture the true prioritization of the vocabulary words when the anchor condition is weakened. In particular, the underspecified models outperform the oracle model. While the correlation with the prioritization scores from SEEK-VEC is only moderate under this condition, the correlation is still higher than that of any of the standard models, including the oracle model, indicating that the signal amplification procedure underlying the ensemble process allows for improved estimation even when the assumptions underlying the component models are violated.

The utility of the SEEK-VEC prioritization scores is explored further in Figure 2c. We calculate the AUC using the prioritization score to predict whether a word is informative (identifying or metainformative) or uninformative combined across 100 simulations. The values along the x -axis show AUC values under the strong anchor condition, and the values along the y -axis show AUC values under the weak anchor condition. Under the strong anchor condition, SEEK-VEC performs as well as the standard oracle model (K6), and outperforms all misspecified models. Under the weak anchor condition, SEEK-VEC significantly outperform all standard models. As predicted by the results from the bottom row of Figure 2c, the underspecified standard models outperform the oracle standard model as well.

#### SEEK-VEC robustly estimates the latent relationships between words

Off-diagonal values in the joint hallmark projection matrix represent grouping scores between vocabulary words, where two words with a high grouping score are frequently co-identified as hallmark words across candidate topic models. More generally, grouping scores measure the strength of the relationship between two words with respect to the underlying latent structure. Patterns of grouping scores can give insight into potential relationships between derived topics, and the structure of these grouping scores can show patterns of topics. Figure 2d shows the correlation of the true grouping scores with the grouping scores from the standard and ensemble estimated hallmark matrices. The top row shows the correlations under the strong-anchor setting; the patterns are very similar to those of the prioritization score correlations. As with the prioritization scores, there is a significant penalty for overspecifying the number of topics under the standard method, but the performance of SEEK-VEC, which includes these overspecified models, does not experience the same drop in performance. The bottom row shows the correlations as the anchor condition weakens. As with the prioritization scores, weaker anchor conditions correspond to lower overall correlations. Again, SEEK-VEC outperforms the standard models, demonstrating that the ensemble method is more robust to weaker signal strength conditions.

#### SEEK-VEC provides a lens for model diagnostics

The output matrix from SEEK-VEC can also be used to assess the stability of a given topic model. Comparing the joint hallmark projection matrix from a standard topic model to the SEEK-VEC output can inform the extent to which the conclusions of the proposed topic model are conditional on the choice of K . For example, suppose O ^ K = 5 is the joint hallmark projection matrix corresponding to a standard topic model with K = 5 topics and O ^ is the output from SEEK-VEC. A high value of O ^ i j K = 5 and low value of O ^ i j indicates that the signal from the K = 5 model may be unique to that particular model and therefore should be interpreted with caution. Further discussion and illustration is found in Section S1.4 and a real data example is found in Section S1.6.

#### SEEK-VEC is robust to hyperparameter selection

There are two hyperparameters required for SEEK-VEC: the choice of values of K to ensemble and the threshold value. Supplemental Figure S3 shows extended results for SEEK-VEC implementations varying both of these parameters, as well as results varying the level of noise in the simulated data. These results show that the performance of SEEK-VEC is negligibly harmed by including additional overspecified models, despite the fact that standard overspecified topic models have very poor performance. The performance of all models is sensitive to the choice of threshold value, or sensitivity, but in all threshold settings, ensembling is preferable to running a misspecified standard topic model (Supplemental Figures S3a and S3b). Further, in the case where signal is weaker and the anchor word condition is more strongly violated, SEEK-VEC can start to outperform the oracle method, demonstrating the value of signal amplification (Supplemental Figures S3c and S3d).

### SEEK-VEC requires minimal additional computational time

Figure 2e shows the additional computational time required by the ensembling step compared to the computational time required by running the component topic models. The rows represent different topic modeling algorithms, and the columns represent different values of the vocabulary size p . For all methods except for Topic-SCORE, the added computational time to run the ensembling step is trivial relative to the time required to run the standard models. For Topic-SCORE, for p ≥ 1000 , the ensembling step using a higher threshold value t can take up to twice as long as running the component models. As shown in Algorithm 3, the input to the spectral ensembling procedure is a set of p * × p * matrices, where p * ≤ p is the number of vocabulary words with non-zero diagonal entries across all component matrices. Therefore, choosing a lower value of t means a smaller value of p * , which means smaller input matrices for the spectral ensembling step. However, the absolute additional time required when using Topic-SCORE to ensemble K = { 3 , … , 12 } , even with larger p and higher threshold value t , is at most just over a minute.

### Prioritization scores and grouping scores assess DSM-5 construct validity in the SPARK Adult Self-Report

The SPARK study is an ongoing autism research study supported by the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative [23]. The study, which has over 100,000 participants with autism, includes both genetic and phenotypic data. One source of phenotypic data is the Adult Self-Report (ASR), a well-validated survey instrument that is part of the Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessment and measures adult psychopathology [24]. For the ASR, individuals are asked to rate themselves on 123 items, with the scoring options of 0 = Not True , 1 = Somewhat or Sometimes True , and 2 = Very True or Often True . Of these items, 69 of the items on the ASR correspond to one of six DSM-5-Oriented Scales: Depressive Problems, Anxiety Problems, Somatic Problems, Avoidant Personality Problems, Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Problems, and Antisocial Personality Problems. Items on these scales were rated to have strong correspondence to DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for particular disorders or categories of disorders [25]. Taking the items as the vocabulary and the individuals as documents, we can analyze the responses on these items from the 1,809 respondents with a confirmed autism diagnosis and assess how well these scales align with behavioral patterns among adults with autism.

Figure 3a shows the heatmap corresponding to O ^ t = 0.5 . We choose a high threshold value in this context because each item is designed to contain signal relating to an underlying pattern, namely the corresponding DSM-5 scale. The heatmap is filtered to rows containing a grouping score of 0.5 or greater, representing a weighted majority consensus of a significant relationship among items. Of the nine items in the Somatic scale, seven appear as a stable block with strong signal and little to no overlap. Of the seven items in the Avoidant scale, only three appear, but they are again stable with strong signal. The remaining items come from both the ADHD and Antisocial scales, and there is significant overlap between markers of these scales. This indicates that scores on these items may be due to shared latent patterns as opposed to distinct ADHD/Antisocial patterns, which aligns with research showing that individuals with ADHD are more likely to engage in antisocial behavior [26, 27]. Notably absent from the filtered heatmap are any items from the Depressive or Anxiety scales. While individuals with autism are four times more likely to experience depression than individuals without autism [28], current diagnostic criteria for depression may not generalize to individuals with autism, for whom depression may present differently [29]. Similarly, while an estimated 50% of individuals with autism experience anxiety, anxiety may have an atypical presentation in these individuals, making standardized criteria such as the DSM-5 ineffective for detecting it [30]. It is not surprising, then, that the DSM-5 Depressive or Anxiety scale items do not appear to present as strong signal of underlying patterns in a respondent population of individuals with autism.

No items on the Depression or Anxiety subscales have a grouping score of 0.5 or greater with any other item. (b) Scatterplot showing the patterns of prioritization versus maximum grouping scores in O ^ t = 0.5 . The dashed lined indicates the filtering threshold for plotting in (a). To further examine each survey item, we can examine their prioritization scores (Figure 3c), which represent the consensus signal strength of the item, as well as each item’s maximum grouping score (Figure 3d), which represents the extent to which it jointly indicates a pattern with at least one other item. Figure 3b shows a scatterplot comparing the prioritization and maximum grouping values, which allows for a classification of the survey items. First, we can notice that many items fall along the diagonal. These survey items have at least one other item with which they are consistently co-identified, regardless of signal strength. For items falling below the diagonal, this means that their co-identification is less consistent: there is no other item with which they are consistently paired. As an example, we can see that q_092_trouble_law (“I do things that may cause me trouble with the law”) has a prioritization score of 1, indicating that it is consistently identified as a hallmark item to an underlying latent pattern of responses. However, its maximum grouping score is less than 1, meaning it is indicative of different patterns in different models. This can be seen visually in Figure 3a, where it shows moderately strong overlap with both the majority-ADHD and majority-Antisocial blocks. Another interesting case is q_029_fears (“I am afraid of certain animals, situations, or places”), which has a prioritization score of 1 but a very low maximum grouping score. This shows that this item is consistently identified as the only hallmark item in a topic. This provides useful insight for survey design: this question seems to be ascertaining a concept that is distinct from the other items, and therefore may be misleading if used in a composite score. Examining the prioritization and grouping scores of these items provides useful insight for appropriate instrument design and construct validity for assessing DSM-5 categories in adults with autism.

### Prioritization scores separate progenitors from progeny in single-cell expression datasets

The development of new single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technologies has led to improved understanding of the developmental trajectory of cells [31]. These methods measure levels of RNA transcription across genes, and the heterogeneity of these expression levels across cells yield insight into the latent dynamic processes underlying cellular differentiation [32]. While the raw output of scRNA-seq data is a matrix of counts, typically the log-transformed data is analyzed to account for the heteroscedasticity of expression between highly- and lowly-expressed genes [33].

Since the data are (transformed) counts, we can analyze scRNA-seq data with SEEK-VEC, treating cells as words and genes as documents. Under this framework, we can consider the topics to be the latent cellular differentiation processes. Each cell’s prioritization score in O ^ estimates its signal strength with respect to the topics, so we would expect that differentiated progeny cells would have larger diagonal values than their less-differentiated progenitors. We apply this method to two murine datasets: one contains 2,730 cells undergoing hematopoiesis [34], shown in Figure 4a, and the other contains 3,542 intestinal stem cells undergoing differentiation [35], shown in Figure 4b. For each dataset, we focus on two differentiation trajectories. For the hematopoiesis dataset, we analyze the diagonal values of the megakaryocyte–erythroid progenitor cells (MEP) and their progeny (Ery/Mk), as well as the granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMP) and their progeny (Mono/Gran). For the intestinal stem cell dataset, we analyze the diagonal values of the transit-amplifying cells (TA) and their progeny (Ecy), as well as the enteroendocrine progenitors (ECP) and their progeny (EC). We compare SEEK-VEC to four popular methods for single-cell analysis: Destiny [36], Palantir [37], PHATE [38], and Slingshot [39].

Figures 4c and 4d show the results comparing the AUCs of each method on the two trajectories per dataset. In both datasets, Palantir and Slingshot perform well on one trajectory and poorly on the other; this suggests that they are less robust to branching structure within the data. In the hematopoiesis data, SEEK-VEC outperforms Destiny and PHATE, and in the intestinal data, the three methods have comparable performance. These results indicate that the prioritization scores of SEEK-VEC successfully capture the degree of signal contained in each cell, thereby separating differentiated progeny cells from their less-differentiated progenitors.

### Grouping scores yield clinically-relevant diet and lifestyle patterns from the UK Biobank Food Preferences questionnaire

Between 2019 and 2020, UK Biobank participants were invited to complete a questionnaire on food and related preferences [40]. Participants were asked to rate 150 items on a scale from 1 (extremely dislike) to 9 (extremely like). By treating the individuals as documents, the survey items as words, and their ratings as counts, we can use topic modeling to detect patterns of preferences, and we can use SEEK-VEC to find robust indicators of these underlying patterns without specifying a number of topics. We analyze the responses from 40,761 unrelated British White individuals and associate the derived blocks of words with clinically-significant health outcomes.

Figure 5 shows the O ^ t = 0.2 matrix derived from the questionnaire data. The matrix is filtered to rows with at least one grouping score of 0.5 of higher; this can be thought of as there being an eigenscore-weighted majority consensus that there is a significant relationship between two words. There are five blocks that clearly emerge in the figure: the first block is about fish, the second block is about exercise-related behaviors, the third block is about spicy foods, the fourth block is about adding sugar to coffee/tea, and the fifth block is about non-wine alcohol preferences. These blocks are all relatively stable: with the possible exception of “baked/steamed fish” and “shellfish (other than prawns)” in the first block, all blocks are well-shaded, indicating that the words are consistently co-identified as representative words across topic models. Additionally, there is no dark shading along the off-diagonal, meaning the blocks seem to fairly consistently represent distinct topics.

To further investigate these topic blocks, we can examine the associations between preferences within these blocks and health outcomes. For each block, we can derive an individual’s preference score by taking their average rating on each of the relevant items, and then standardizing by their mean rating score across all items. The purpose of the standardization is to ensure that we are assessing relative preferences, since different individuals might have a different perception of what a score of 5 is, for example. We then run regression models evaluating the association between these scores and health outcomes among the 40,761 individuals: incident chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD; n cases = 300 ), dementia ( n cases = 82 ) , myocardial infarction ( ( n cases = 323 ) , and stroke ( n cases = 234 ) , as well as statin-adjusted log triglyceride, HDL, and LDL levels. The models are adjusted for age, sex, BMI, low vs. moderate/high physical activity, ever vs. never smoking, and socioeconomic status via the Townsend deprivation index, and the results are shown in Table 1. Some of the results can be reasonably interpreted in the context of the foods and behaviors comprising each block. For example, a higher score on the block representing a preference for fish is associated with lower odds of dementia, which aligns with the known association between increased fish consumption and lower likelihood of cognitive decline [41].

However, it is important to note that the observed associations may not necessarily be attributable solely to the foods comprising the blocks; rather, these blocks and behaviors act as indicators of underlying patterns of preferences. For example, a preference for adding sugar into one’s coffee or tea could be indicative of a sweet tooth and therefore higher carbohydrate intake, which would explain the association with lower levels of HDL [42]. Similarly, of the five blocks, scores on the exercise-related block are the only ones with a positive correlation with either “fruit” or “vegetables”. Particularly since these models control for physical activity, significant associations with this block score may be due more to the latent patterns that these scores indicate rather than the block-specific behaviors themselves. Another possible example of this is the statistically significant reduction in odds of dementia associated with a higher preference score for non-wine alcohol. Given the association between social isolation and dementia [43], as well as the function of pubs as a social outlet for elderly individuals in the UK [44], the latent pattern indicated by the fifth block may also indicate reduced levels of social isolation.

In keeping with the interpretation of the joint hallmark projection matrix, the blocks are the most reliable indicators of the latent patterns of preferences. The ability to find these stable indicators is highly beneficial for improving efficiency in survey design. An analogue to the traditional topic modeling setting is the identification of anchor words, where locating an anchor word in a document is a strong indicator of the respective topic in that document. Likewise, since SEEK-VEC is able to identify stable indicators of health-relevant preference patterns, survey items can be refined and prioritized to reduce administrative burden and cost.

## Discussion

Topic modeling is a powerful tool for detecting latent substructure in count data. However, standard topic models require choosing a number of topics K , which may not be possible in non-text data settings, such as symptom data or gene expression data, either due to a lack of interpretability of the candidate topic models or weaker signal strength in the absence of the anchor word condition. SEEK-VEC is a robust method for uncovering this latent structure that does not require choosing a single number of topics and performs better than standard models in weaker signal strength scenarios. As shown through simulations, SEEK-VEC can accurately and robustly estimate the true prioritization and grouping scores, which classify the vocabulary words and capture the relationships among the words, respectively. When applied to the SPARK Autism Self-Report survey data, SEEK-VEC yields insights into the construct validity of the DSM-V psychopathology scales applied to a population of adults with autism. Analyzing the UK Biobank food preferences questionnaire with SEEK-VEC yields indicators of underlying dietary and behavioral patterns that are significantly associated with incident health outcomes and lipid traits. SEEK-VEC also achieves performance equivalent to that of leading single-cell gene expression methods for distinguishing differentiated cells from their progenitors based on the strength of signal represented by each cell’s diagonal value.

An important limitation of SEEK-VEC is that it requires the construction and analysis of p × p matrices. As such, the method is best suited for high-dimensional settings where p ≪ n . This makes this method particularly fitting for health data contexts, such as surveys with many more respondents than items, or single-cell applications where there are many more genes than cells and the interest is in the latent structure of the cells, as in the previous example. However, if the interest were in the latent structure of the genes, the ensembling would be very computationally intensive. One potential area for future development with this method that may make it more suitable for large- p contexts is to instead ensemble the latent subspace in which O ^ can be thought of as a distance matrix. For example, examining the principal components of O ^ may yield branching structure within the matrix, which could be particularly useful in a single-cell developmental trajectory context.

Another avenue for future exploration with SEEK-VEC is its utility for understanding the behavior of black-box algorithms with respect to their hyperparameters. AI-based methods such as BERTopic [45] lack a statistical framework and can be seen as black-box methods, meaning it can be challenging to assess the stability and reliability of the output [46, 47]. SEEK-VEC holds promise as a non-parametric tool to analyze the stability of the output of black-box models with respect to their hyperparameters without requiring any statistical framework for the method itself.

## Methods and Materials

### Topic Modeling Framework

Given n observed documents written on a vocabulary of p words, Let D ∈ R p × n be a matrix comprising the counts of each vocabulary word in each document. Let A ∈ R p × K be a latent matrix representing each vocabulary word’s weight on each of K topics, such that A 1 , … , A K , the columns of A , represent probability mass functions on the vocabulary. A word in the vocabulary is defined as an anchor word if its corresponding row in the A matrix has only one non-zero entry; these words can be thought to identify the topics. Let W ∈ R K × n be another latent matrix which represents the mixture of topics within each document, with w i ( k ) representing the weight of document i on topic k . For a document i of length N i , topic modeling posits that the i -th column of D is drawn as N i d i ~ Multinomial N i , ∑ k = 1 K w i ( k ) A k . This yields the following relationship:

$$ E [ D ] = A W $$

Since typically K ≪ n , this implies a low-rank structure underlying D [10].

### Topic-SCORE

Topic-SCORE is a state-of-the-art method for topic modeling that uses singular value decomposition and simplex geometry to estimate the low-rank A from D [10]. After initial normalization of the observed D matrix to account for word frequency heterogeneity, Topic-SCORE obtains the matrix of the K left singular vectors Ξ = ξ 1 … ξ K . The rows of Ξ are contained in a simplicial cone with K supporting rays, where the anchor words lie on the supporting rays. Next, to compress the simplicial cone into a simplex, Ξ is normalized via SCORE normalization: each row is normalized by its first component, yielding R ∈ R p × ( K - 1 ) . Each row of R represents a low-dimensional embedding of a word into R K - 1 . The anchor words, which were located on the supporting rays of the K -dimensional simplicial cone, are now located at the vertices of the ( K - 1 ) -dimensional simplex. These vertices are found using a vertex hunting step, and since these vertices identify the location of the pure topics, each vocabulary word’s weight on each topic can be found by uncovering the convex combination of vertices that yields its position in the simplex, thus yielding the desired low-rank matrix A ∈ R p × K . Importantly, misspecifying K implies the embedding of the vocabulary onto a space with the incorrect number of dimensions; the impact of this misspecification is further explored in Figure S5.

### Details of SEEK-VEC

The target estimand in topic modeling is A , a p × K matrix representing the weight of each of p words on each of K topics. Each column of A represents a probability mass function (PMF) on the vocabulary, with the most frequently-used words per topic having the highest probability. This means that the rows of A corresponding to common words such as “and” or “the” will have high probabilities in each column, despite not being useful for the identification or interpretation of the topics. Thus, in practice, what is usually used for the interpretation of the topics is a row-normalized version of A called the topic loadings matrix [1]. Each row of the topic loadings matrix represents the relative weights of each topic for each word.

The “representative words” for each topic are found by identifying the words in the topic loadings matrix with the largest values [10]. This can be done in several ways, such as choosing the top n words per column or by choosing the n words with the largest values across the entire topic loadings matrix. The advantage of the former strategy is that it ensures the same number of representative words per topic and prevents a topic with many strong representative words from dominating the interpretation; the advantage for the latter strategy is it avoids inflating the importance of relatively unimportant words in the case where a given topic has fewer truly informative words than others. We can represent this differentiation process between representative words and uninformative words as a dichotomizing of the topic loadings matrix to the hallmark matrix H . In this matrix, h i j = 1 if word i is representative for topic j , and 0 otherwise. This yields the joint hallmark projection matrix O = H H ⊤ .

In order to understand the topic structure with respect to the vocabulary without knowing K , we can estimate O ∈ R p × p by combining the insights of a variety of candidate topic models. To develop an estimator of O , we propose the following spectral ensembling method:

Let 𝒦 = 3 , … , K * be a collection of candidate topic counts. For each k ∈ 𝒦 , let A ^ k be the topic matrix derived from running Topic-SCORE with k topics. Let O ^ k be the corresponding joint hallmark projection matrix.

Define the similarity matrix G ∈ R | 𝒦 | × | 𝒦 | where

$$ G i , j = t r O ^ k i ⊤ O ^ k j , $$

which measures the similarity between the joint hallmark projection matrix O ^ k i using k i topics and the joint hallmark projection matrix O ^ k j using k j topics. Let u 1 ∈ R | 𝒦 | be the leading eigenvector of G . Then we can combine the | 𝒦 | joint hallmark projection matrices as follows:

$$ Ω ^ = ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 u 1 k u 1 1 O ^ k $$

The resulting matrix Ω ^ is a consensus-weighted combination of the joint hallmark projection matrices from the candidate topic models (Algorithm 3). Since Ω ^ is a weighted combination of integer-valued matrices, it will not itself necessarily (or likely) be integer-valued. However, as is shown, it can still be used as a guide to identifying topic-relevant vocabulary words and labeling the topics.

This spectral ensembling method generalizes the spectral meta-learner method of Parisi et al. (2014) [48] and the eigenscore method of Ma et al. (2023) [21]. Both methods address the question of the best way to combine candidate models via a consensus-based weighting, where the leading eigenvector of a matrix summarizing the differences among the models provides an optimal weighting. However, a key difference in this setting is that the topics from candidate models can be mixtures of the oracle model [10], which violates the uncorrelatedness assumption of the previous two methods. The default topic modeling method used in this paper is Topic-SCORE; however, alternate methods can be used if desired.

### Method Implementation

The overview of the implementation of SEEK-VEC is given in Algorithm 1. As with standard topic modeling methods, the method requires the word-document corpus matrix D as input. The method also requires 𝒦 , which is a list of candidate topic counts to ensemble. Finally, the method requires t , the parameter for thresholding the topic loadings matrices. Details of this procedure are shown in Algorithm 2, which involves converting each output A matrix to a topic loadings matrix by normalizing the rows to sum to 1. The loading matrix is then converted to a binary matrix through the thresholding procedure, which is then transpose-multiplied by itself to obtain a p × p matrix that is free of k and can thus be ensembled through the spectral ensembling procedure. This procedure, shown in more detail in Algorithm 3, is optimized for computational efficiency through a Zero-Reduce procedure. For this step, any vocabulary word which has a diagonal value of 0 across all candidate matrices is removed prior to calculating the G ∈ R | 𝒦 | × | 𝒦 | matrix, since any weighted sum of the candidate matrices will result in zeroes across the rows and columns of these vocabulary words. Once G is calculated, the candidate matrices are combined in a weighted sum proportional to the leading eigenvector of G . The output of the algorithm is the ensemble hallmark matrix Ω . The prioritization score for the i th vocabulary word is Ω i i , and the grouping score for the i th and j th vocabulary words is Ω i j = Ω j i .

## Abstract

Background Associations between dairy intake and body composition, and cardiometabolic traits have

been inconsistently observed in epidemiological studies, and the causal relationship remains ill-defined.

Methods We performed a Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis using an established genetic variant

located upstream of the lactase gene (LCT-13910 C/T, rs4988235) associated with dairy intake as an

instrumental variable (IV). The causal effects of dairy intake on body composition, and cardiometabolic

traits (lipids, glycemic traits, and inflammatory factors) were quantified by IV estimators among 182,041

participants from 18 studies.

Results High dairy intake was associated with higher lean mass (β=0.117 kg per serving/day, SE: 0.035;

P=0.001) and higher HbA1c (β=0.009 [0.002] % per serving/day, P<0.001), but lower LDL (β=-0.014

[0.006] mmol/L per serving/day, P=0.013), TC (β=-0.012 [0.005] mmol/L per serving/day, P=0.023), and

non-HDL (β=-0.012 [0.005] mmol/L per serving/day, P=0.028). The LCT -13910 C/T CT+TT genotype

was associated with 0.214 more dairy servings per day (SE=0.047, P<0.001), 0.284 cm higher waist

circumference (SE=0.118, P=0.017) and 0.112 kg higher lean mass (SE=0.027, P=3.8×10-5), but 0.032

mmol/L lower LDL (SE=0.009, P=0.001), and 0.032 mmol/L lower TC (SE=0.010, P=0.001).

Genetically higher dairy intake was associated with increased waist circumference (β=1.327 [0.623] cm

per serving/day, P=0.020) and increased lean mass (β=0.523 [0.170] kg per serving/day, P=0.002), but

decreased LDL (β=-0.150 [0.053] mmol/L per serving/day, P=0.005), and TC (β=-0.150 [0.057] mmol/L

per serving/day, P=0.008); whereas no associations of the genetically higher dairy intake with glycemic

traits were found (all P>0.05). Results for lean mass remained significant at P=0.002 after correction for

multiple testing (0.05/18).

Conclusions The present study provides evidence to support a causal effect of higher dairy intake on

increased lean mass and suggestively decreased LDL and TC among adults. Our findings imply that the

observational associations of dairy intake with glycemic traits could be the result of confounding.

## Introduction

Observational studies and randomized control trails (RCTs) showed mixed results for associations of

dairy intake with body composition,1-7 lipids8, glucose8 9, and inflammatory biomarkers10, in which

reverse causation, residual confounding, and limited generalizability are often nonnegligible.11 Mendelian

randomization (MR) analysis,9 12-14  which is analogous to an RCT where randomization to genotype takes

place at conception,15 has been widely used to assess potential causal associations of lifetime variations of

modifiable factors with diseases.12 16-21

Previous large scaled MR analyses, adopting an well-established genetic marker (LCT-13910 C/T

rs4988235) as an instrument variable for dairy intake, demonstrated that high dairy intake associated with

higher BMI,19 but not causally related to hypertension,12 diabetes,13 and cardiovascular diseases.9 14

However, whether dairy intake is causally associated with body composition and other important

cardiometabolic traits is largely unknown.

Therefore, in the current study, we further performed a MR analysis using an established dairy intake

associated genetic variant near the lactase gene LCT among 182,041 adult participants from 18 cohorts to

examine the causal association of habitual dairy intake with body composition and cardiometabolic traits

such as lipids, glycemic traits and inflammatory factors in general populations.

## Methods

Study participants

The study was conducted within the Mendelian Randomization of Dairy Consumption Working Group,

represented here by 18 cohort studies and up to 182,041 individuals. Supplemental Table 1 presents

detailed descriptions of each study. Participants from each study provided written, informed consent, and

ethical approval was granted by local institutional review boards (Supplemental Table 2).


<!-- Page 4 -->


4

Dairy intake assessment and outcomes

Intake of dairy products was collected by self-reported questionnaire in each study; detailed information

on cohort-specific data collection methods is provided in Supplemental Table 3. Total dairy products

included ‘skim/low fat milk’, ‘whole milk’, ‘ice cream’, ‘yogurt’, ‘cottage/ricotta cheese’, ‘cream cheese’,

‘other cheese’, and ‘cream’. The primary outcomes are body composition (body fat percentage, waist

circumference waist: hip ratio, lean mass, and fat mass) and cardiometabolic traits (lipids (high density

lipoprotein [HDL], low density lipoprotein [LDL], total cholesterol [TC], total triglyceride [TG], Non-

HDL, apoB), glycemic traits (fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin, insulin resistance, and insulin

sensitivity), and inflammatory factors (regular C reactive protein [CRP] and high sensitive CRP

[hsCRP]) at baseline or in the follow-up. Detailed information on the outcome measure for each study is

reported in Supplemental Table 4.

SNP selection and genotyping methods

In the present study, we chose the widely confirmed and extensively studied variant (LCT-13910 C/T

rs4988235) as the instrumental variable (IV) for dairy intake.13 14 22 The variant rs4988235, located

upstream from the LCT gene, is associated with lactase persistence and thereby with the ability to digest

lactose, the primary source of carbohydrates in milk.23 The TT and TC genotypes are associated with

lactase persistence and CC with non-persistence. Therefore, lactase persistence is a dominantly inherited

genetic trait. Most studies used direct genotype information on rs4988235 from previously genotyped

array data. Whenever rs4988235 was not genotyped directly, we used either (i) the HapMap II CEU

(European) reference panel-imputed genetic information for rs4988235 or (ii) genotype information of

proxy that are in high linkage disequilibrium (LD) with rs4988235 (n = 5, r2>0.9). Genotyping platforms,

genotype frequencies, Hardy Weinberg equilibrium P values, and call rates (median of 98.8%) for LCT -

13910 C/T are listed in Supplemental Table 5.


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

Statistical analysis

Our study tested: 1) the observational associations of dairy intake associated with body composition,

lipids, glycemic traits, and inflammatory factors; 2) the genetic associations of the LCT -13910 C/T

rs4988235 with dairy intake and cardiometabolic traits under a dominant model (CC vs. CT+TT) as

lactase persistence is a dominantly inherited genetic trait; 3) the causal effect of dairy intake on

cardiometabolic traits by using the IV estimator.

A standard analysis protocol was applied to each individual study to produce comparable results. Linear

regression was used to test the observational associations of dairy intake with cardiometabolic traits after

adjustment for age, sex, ethnicity, region, years of follow-up, and other baseline covariates (smoking

status, physical activity, total energy intake, and alcohol intake), as available. Linear regression was used

to test the genetic associations of LCT -13910 C/T with dairy intake or cardiometabolic traits after

adjustment for age, sex, ethnicity, region, and total energy.

Meta-analysis and between-study heterogeneity

Meta-analyses were conducted using individual participant data in each study, then, pooled β coefficients

across studies, using random-effects or fixed-effects meta-analysis. We assessed between-study

heterogeneity via Cochrane’s Q- and I2-statistics.24-26 We used random-effects meta-analysis if I2>0.25, or

fixed-effects model will be used.27

Standard errors and inference for the instrumental variable (IV) estimator

After meta-analysis, we used the IV estimators to quantify the strength of the causal association of dairy

## Results

Baseline characteristics of participating studies

Baseline characteristics of the 182,041participants from 18 studies are shown in Table 1 and

Supplemental Tables 6, 7 & 8. A description of each study and additional characteristics of participants

are presented in Supplemental Tables 1 & 6. A total of 17 studies provided data for LCT -13910 C/T, and

one study (ARIC-AA) provided results for the proxy SNP rs1446585 (defined on the basis of r2 ≥ 0.90

with rs4988235 in individuals. Chi-square tests showed that the CCHS, CGPS, and FamHS did not

achieve Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) (Supplemental Table 5).

Observational associations of dairy intake with cardiometabolic traits

Our meta-analysis showed that high dairy intake was significantly associated with higher lean mass

(β=0.117 kg per serving/day, SE: 0.035; P=0.001) and higher HbA1c (β=0.009 % per serving/day, SE:

0.002; P<0.001), but lower LDL (β=-0.014 mmol/L per serving/day, SE: 0.006; P=0.013), TC (β=-0.012


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

mmol/L per serving/day, SE: 0.005; P=0.023), and non-HDL (β=-0.012 mmol/L per serving/day, SE:

0.005; P=0.028) (Figure 2).

Genetic association of the LCT -13910 C/T with dairy intake and cardiometabolic traits

In a dominant model, we found that the LCT -13910 C/T CT+TT genotype was significantly associated

with 0.214 more dairy servings per day (β=0.214 serving/day; SE=0.047; P=6.8×10-6). We pooled the

genetic association with cardiometabolic traits using fixed- or random-effects meta-analysis, and found

that the LCT -13910 C/T CT+TT genotype was significantly associated with 0.284 cm higher waist

circumference (β=0.284; SE=0.118; P=0.017) and 0.112 kg higher lean mass (β=0.112; SE=0.027; P=3.8

×10-5), but 0.032 mmol/L lower LDL (β=-0.032 mmol/L per serving/day, SE: 0.009; P=0.001), and

0.032 mmol/L lower TC (β=-0.032 mmol/L per serving/day, SE: 0.010; P=0.001) (Figure 3).

Instrumental variable estimated causality between dairy intake and cardiometabolic traits

*Figure 3 presents the genetic association with cardiometabolic traits, and the IV estimated causal effects*

of dairy intake on cardiometabolic traits. Increases in genetically determined dairy intake was associated

with increased waist circumference (β=1.327 cm per serving/day; SE=0.623; P=0.020) and increased lean

mass (β=0.523 kg per serving/day; SE=0.170; P=0.002), but decreased LDL (β=-0.150 mmol/L per

serving/day, SE: 0.053; P=0.005), TC (β=-0.150 mmol/L per serving/day, SE: 0.057; P=0.008). After

correction for multiple testing, MR association of dairy intake with lean mass remained significant at

P=0.002 (0.05/18). However, we did not observe significant associations of genetically determined dairy

intake with other cardiometabolic traits (Figure 3).

We further conducted stratified analyses of estimated causality by age, follow-up years, study design,

ethnic group and CC genotype frequency (Table 2). Significant MR associations of genetically

determined dairy intake on LDL and TC were only observed in studies with mean age equal and more

than 50 years, and follow-up time less than 5 years.

## Discussion

In thus far the largest MR analysis study, including 182,041 adults from 18 cohorts, our results support a

causal relation between higher dairy intake and increased lean mass, and suggestively decreased LDL and

TC levels. In addition, our findings imply that the observational associations of dairy intake with

glycemic traits could be the result of confounding.

In our well-powered study, we individually analyzed 182,041 individuals and provided strong evidence

that high dairy intake was causally associated with higher lean mass. Results from our MR and

multivariable analyses were highly consistent, both suggesting higher lean mass in those eating more

dairy products. In line with our findings, a previous meta-analysis of RCTs showed that dairy

consumption increased lean mass.4 Several mechanisms might be underlined for the impact of dairy

intake on the regulation of lean mass. First, increased protein intake from dairy products may promote

maintenance of lean mass.30 Second, hormone estrone found in dairy products may promote increases in

body weight.19 31 32 Third, higher intake of dairy foods is associated with higher plasma insulin-like

growth factor-I, which may contribute to weight gain.19 33 However, future research is needed to further

illustrate precise mechanisms of dairy products on body composition in the context of energy restriction.

By using the LCT -13910 C/T as an instrument for dairy intake, our MR results indicated that higher dairy

intake is marginally associated with decreased TC and LDL levels. Observational evidence from

Mediterranean, Danish and American populations suggested that milk intake was also not associated with

lipids.9 14 However, one meta-analysis of controlled short-term probiotic milk product intervention studies

showed that the fermented yogurt product was related to a 4% decrease in TC and a 5% decrease in LDL-

C.34 Thus, probiotic milk product, especially fermented yogurt that drives the protective effect on lipids. It


<!-- Page 9 -->


9

worth noting that using the LCT -13910 C/T as an IV of dairy intake in general, rather than milk

specifically, making our results interpreting difficulty. Previous studies indicated that the association

between this genetic variant is specific to milk,11 possibly because of probiotics in some nonmilk dairy

(such as yogurt and fermented milk) that may facilitate the digestion of lactose and/or differences in

lactose concentration. In the current study, the use of total dairy products including skim/ low-fat milk,

whole milk, ice cream, yogurt, cottage/ricotta cheese, cream cheese, other cheese, and cream, may largely

attenuate our findings. Future study on the causal relationship between dairy-specific product and lipids

were wanted.

We did not find the causal relevance of dairy intake with glycemic traits such as fasting glucose, insulin,

insulin sensitivity and insulin resistance. Likewise, previous MR analyses demonstrated genetically high

milk intake also did not influence plasma levels of glucose.9 14 Our findings were also supported by a 3-

week randomized crossover study indicating that both whole milk and skimmed milk did not affect

fasting blood lipids, glucose, or insulin in healthy adults.8 Our MR results may potentially explained the

non-significant causal effect of high milk intake on risk of type 2 diabetes.13 However, previous MR

analysis observed a significant sex difference in genetic association with fasting glucose; the T-allele was

significantly associated with lower fasting glucose in women, but not in men. The association in women,

where the T-allele associated with higher milk intake is inversely associated with fasting glucose.9 Further

investigations are needed to explore this possible sex difference.

Several strengths merit consideration. First, in the present consortium-based effort involving 18 studies,

we used a standardized analysis plan, thus less likely to be affected by publication bias than meta-

analyses based on published reports. The large sample size allowed us to assess the consistency of

associations across a number of studies and to gain sufficient power for conclusive estimation of causal

effect. Second, the lactose-tolerance variant is a well-established genetic marker for dairy intake, with

solid biological basis and, therefore, a valid instrumental variable for dairy intake.12-14 19 The instrument


<!-- Page 10 -->


10

for carrying out this MR study has largely prevented potentially distorting influences and is of great

benefit for future decision-making upon the development of novel behavioral interventions.

Despite the convincing concept of MR analysis, several limitations have to be taken into consideration

while interpreting our results. First, the MR study added to established study designs such as RCT

without the ability to fully replace them. Second, we could not exclude the possibility of pleiotropic

effects of the LCT genotype (a gene affects 2 or more apparently unrelated phenotypic traits). However, to

our knowledge, no pleiotropic effect has been reported previously. This genetic variant is specific to milk,

at least has a stronger association with milk,11 therefore, the use of total dairy products including may

largely attenuate our findings. Furthermore, the associations of LCT genotype with lactase persistence and

milk intake vary across populations. Although the LCT -13910 C/T is highly associated with lactase

persistence and dairy intake in northern European populations, its association with dairy intake is not

universal.35 Other SNPs, including MCM6 rs3754686 at intron 15, occur more frequently in some global

regions,36, therefore, represent plausible alternatives in diverse cohorts. Hence, bias from population

stratification is deemed likely.

In summary, the present study suggests a causal effect of higher dairy intake on increased lean mass and

suggestively decreased LDL and TC. Our findings also suggest that the observational associations of

dairy intake with glycemic traits could be the result of confounding. Our results emphasize that high

intake of dairy may promote the maintenance of lean mass and an improved lipid profile.

*Figure 1. A schematic description of a Mendelian randomization analysis.*

MR can be used to test the hypothesis that exposure (dairy intake) causes outcomes (cardiometabolic

traits). Three assumptions of MR: 1) Genetic variants must be associated with dairy intake; 2) Genetic

variants must not be associated with confounders; 3) Genetic variants must influence cardiometabolic

traits only through dairy intake, not through other pathways.

The instrumental variable estimator was used to quantify the strength of the causal association of dairy

intake with cardiometabolic traits using LCT -13910 C/T as an instrumental variable.

*Figure 2 Association between dairy intake and cardiometabolic traits among 182,041 participants*

from 18 studies.

Linear regression was used to test the association of dairy intake (serving/day) with cardiometabolic traits

after adjustment of sex, ethnicity, region, years of follow-up, and other baseline covariates if available

(age, smoking status, physical activity, total energy intake, and alcohol intake) in each study. We pooled β

coefficients across studies using random-effect (I2≥25%) or fixed-effect (I2<25%) meta-analyses based on

the heterogeneity between studies.

*Figure 2 Genetic association and estimated causality between dairy intake and cardiometabolic*

traits.

The LCT-13910 C/T located in upstream of the lactase (LCT) gene was selected as an instrumental

variable. The MR estimate was computed from the ratio of the coefficient of the association between the

LCT -13910 C/T and cardiometabolic traits to that of the association between the LCT -13910 C/T and

dairy intake. This IV estimate reflects the potential causal effect of dairy intake on BMI. We pooled β

coefficients across studies using random-effect (I2≥25%) or fixed-effect (I2<25%) meta-analyses based on

the heterogeneity between studies.

Abstract 205

Endometriosis is a common condition associated with debilitating pelvic pain and infertility. 206

A genome-wide association study meta-analysis, including 60,674 cases and 701,926 207

controls of European and East Asian descent, identified 42 genome-wide significant loci 208

comprising 49 distinct association signals. Effect sizes were largest for stage III/IV disease, 209

driven by ovarian endometriosis. Identified signals explained up to 5.01% of disease 210

variance and regulated expression or methylation of genes in endometrium and blood, 211

many of which were associated with pain perception/maintenance (SRP14/BMF, GDAP1, 212

MLLT10, BSN, NGF). We observed significant genetic correlations between endometriosis 213

and 11 pain-conditions including migraine, back, and multisite chronic pain (MCP), as well as 214

inflammatory conditions including asthma and osteoarthritis. Multi-trait genetic analyses 215

identified substantial sharing of variants associated with endometriosis and MCP/migraine. 216

Targeted investigations of genetically regulated mechanisms shared between endometriosis 217

and other pain-conditions are needed to aid the development of new treatments and 218

facilitate early symptomatic intervention. 219
